Understanding and measuring the magnetic field on open flares surfaces relies on mapping observed values, however, due to observation limitations, the bulk of flares' cores remain unclear and are likely highly magnetic. The current approach to reconstructing global map images ignores the "hidden" core areas' magnetism, yet it has been proposed that accounting for the fill fraction of magnetic fields could significantly improve accuracy. To test this, we used a simple model to create synthetic data, and then solved the inversion problem as we would a real-world scenario, without explicitly accounting for the fill fraction and with fraction inclusion. The resulting image and the fill fraction are then compared to the original parameters. We found that the fill fraction can be recovered from the core areas, however, the presence of bright loops in the middle regions of flares makes the problem more complex. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that without accounting for the fill fraction, the inversion of data from fully magnetic regions yields inaccurate results. Therefore, we propose a new inversion method that explicitly includes the fill fraction, and applies it to three individual flares, two with extremely high fill fractions, and resulted in more precise assessments of the beta and gamma components of the magnetic field. The new method has been found to be highly effective in areas with strong magnetism. It is, however, important to note that the new algorithm needs adjustments when applied to lower fill fraction areas, however, it could be an important improvement for the analysis of flares with highly magnetic cores and upper levels of solar flux tubes. The new method also offers the advantage of allowing for the estimation of the fill fraction from measurements, however, it does require further development to improve the spatial resolution of the image reconstruction. We define a Coxeter group's wedge as a group generated by a specified set of elements, whose mutual reflection properties mirror those of a given Coxeter system. We then establish the concept of a Coxeter system's sphere, which represents the union of reflections about which the original generating set resembles a geometric pattern. We demonstrate that within any Coxeter group's wedge, there exists a largest possible sphere that is also a subgroup. Furthermore, we prove that this maximal sphere's association with any of its reflecting elements is identical to the relationship between the corresponding element and its mirror in the original Coxeter system. We also show that the spheres within the wedge share a hierarchical structure, with each sphere being a subgroup of the preceding one, until they reach the group's root system's Borel subgroup. We further demonstrate that the relationship between these subgroups and the Borel subgroup is analogous to that between the group's root nodes at different levels of a tree. We also discover that the sphere's relationship with the group's itself is analogous to that of the Borel subgroup's relationship with the group. We conclude by illustrating this concept using the $S_n$ Coxeter group, and we also establish that the largest sphere's index within the group determines the group's growth rate. We also discover that the index of the Borel subgroup's largest sphere provides significant insight into the group's geometry and its associated complex, as well as giving a criterion for distinguishing between finite and infinite Coxeter groups. We apply this concept to analyze the group's geometry and its associated complex for both finite and infinite Coxeter groups, including the $S_n$ group, the Artamonov-Rukhlipper group, and the Grigiscenko group. We demonstrate that the group's geometry and its associated complex can be classified based on its root system's tree structure. We also establish that the Artamonov-Rukhlipper group's geometry and its associated complex are identical to those of the $S_n$ group, whereas the Grigiscenko group's geometry and its associated complex are disparate. We conclude by examining the implication of the group's geometry on its associated complex in relation to its root system. We also investigate the association between the group's geometry and its growth rate. We also investigate the association between the group's geometry and its associated complex's Asymptotic Invariant, as well as its impact on the group itself. We also explore the applicability of this concept to other groups that exhibit a Borel hierarchy structure.

Our proposed Generation Architecture for Stream Processing (GASP) serves as a framework that generates efficient numerical routines for stream processing tasks, especially those involving time series data. Our implementation, called LifeStream, takes the form of a numerical library that is highly optimized for various hardware platforms. In contrast to other highly optimized numerical libraries, LifeStream takes up significantly less memory while maintaining comparable performance levels. Furthermore, through the evaluation of LifeStream against other optimized numerical libraries on real-world datasets, it has shown equivalent performance levels and even surpasses some of these libraries in certain aspects. In the specific case of TensorFlow's Multilayer RNN example, it has been found that LifeStream uses approximately 3.85 times less memory than other optimized numerical libraries on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. Additionally, the development of LifeStream has been contributed to the StreamProc repository, a community-driven initiative that fosters the open development of stream processing algorithms and numerical libraries. In its current state, LifeStream provides a notable example of how machine learning models can be accurately replicated using significantly reduced resources. In one example, it has been shown that the replication of a particular machine learning model requires approximately 1.83 times less memory than the original implementation. In the process of developing LifeStream, it has been found that certain optimization strategies that were initially thought to be critical, such as the use of blocking algorithms and memory reclamation mechanisms, may not be necessary for the efficient execution of stream processing tasks, provided the underlying hardware supports it. In particular, it has been observed that the use of blocking algorithms and memory reclamation mechanisms may lead to poor performance on certain hardware platforms, specifically those that use a stack-based memory model, such as certain ARM architectures. Consequently, LifeStream is configured to use unblocking algorithms and a circular buffer memory management system, which enables the library to run efficiently on a wide range of hardware platforms, including those that use a stack-based memory model, such as certain ARM architectures, without the need for memory reclamation mechanisms. Moreover, due to its memory-efficient design, LifeStream can efficiently handle large datasets that would otherwise be too large for other highly optimized numerical libraries, even on high-end GPUs. In one example, it has been found that LifeStream is capable of handling a dataset that is approximately 10 times larger than the maximum capacity of other highly optimized numerical libraries on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. This study develops a comprehensive thermomechanical model to capture the thermosensitive and temperature-dependent properties of polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization. The model's effectiveness in capturing thermomechanical behavior is validated by a parametric study. A magnetic susceptibility expression has been developed for the susceptible phase of a superconducting material with a generic Fermi surface, allowing for analysis of the susceptibility's behavior in various crystallographic environments. The framework focuses on the meager signal phase near the superconducting critical point and is based on a expansion of the free energy around the point of a vanishing magnetic field. The approach facilitates study of the susceptibility's topological dependencies on the Fermi surface, which can be evaluated using a novel integral related to a class of surface integrals over the Fermi surface. These surface integrals, denoted as $\Psi_\Gamma$, are defined by integrating the square root of an algebraic equation derived from the expansion of the free energy. They provide a crucial topological indicator, with which the susceptibility can be distinguished in different topological states and it is proposed that they be referred to as "topological indicators of the Fermi surface" ($\Psi_\Gamma$). The proposed name is demonstrated by calculating the $\Psi_\Gamma$ values for several elements and compounds and it is found that they directly correlate with the strength of the susceptibility in the meager signal phase. Consequently, elements and compounds with the same $\Psi_\Gamma$ value will exhibit similar susceptibility characteristics, whereas those with different $\Psi_\Gamma$ values will exhibit distinct characteristics, indicating that the topological indicators of the Fermi surface hold significant predictive power for the susceptibility in superconducting materials. The proposed name is further validated by analyzing the results and it is found that the $\Psi_\Gamma$ values remain unchanged in different crystallographic environments. The method presents several advantages over the conventional approach to studying the susceptibility near the superconducting critical point, as it enables study of the susceptibility in the meager signal phase without requiring the expansion of the free energy around the point of a vanishing magnetic field, rather it is derived directly from the total free energy of the system. The proposed name is also related to the established indicators of the topological dependencies of the energy levels on the crystallographic environment, which are denoted as $\Psi_K$. The main difference between the two indicators is the presence of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya antiferromagnetic interaction in the $\Psi_\Gamma$ calculation, which is absent in the $\Psi_K$ calculation, indicating that the $\Psi_\Gamma$ values can distinguish between different types of topological dependencies on the Fermi surface. The method is demonstrated by calculating the free energy of a one-dimensional tight-binding model

In this paper, we investigate the validity of this condition for compressible systems at constant pressure through the adiabatic expansion scenario. By examining the conditions under which the system remains multiphase during expansion, we establish a criterion based on the adiabatic compressibility and the ideal gas compressibility. Our results demonstrate that the range of valid chemical potential values becomes increasingly narrow as the system's adiabatic compressibility increases. We have also derived an expression for the maximum variation of chemical potential, which we apply to evaluate the ensemble ensemble's ensemble width and height ratio in compressible systems. Furthermore, we analyze the ensemble width/height ratio ratio's asymptotic behaviors at both narrow and broad distribution limits. Our study reveals that the ensemble width/height ratio ratio approaches the canonical ensemble width/height ratio ratio as the system's adiabatic compressibility tends to zero, while it approaches the ideal gas width/height ratio ratio as the system's adiabatic compressibility becomes large. Our research provides a compressibility-based approach to assessing the ensemble's validity and serves as a bridge between equilibrium coexistence conditions and non-equilibrium evolution scenarios. If-then relation if implied by a sentence is considered a fundamental concept in natural language processing that helps various applications such as knowledge base completion and question answering. Most current approaches label each sentence individually, without accounting for the overall pattern of if-then relations within a text. Our research proposes a novel method called Pattern-Aware Neural Reader, which incorporates the underlying structure of if-then relations, represented as a directed graph, into the neural reader model. By integrating the graph, the model gains a better understanding of text by recognizing the relationships between key phrases, without requiring explicit extraction. When applied to a task where the goal is to identify entities connected by specific relations to entities already identified, the model performs significantly better than the baseline models, including a strong competitor with self-supervised pre-training capabilities. Furthermore, our model demonstrates the ability to train on general if-then relation types and generalize to novel types, achieving a notable gain of 12% F1-score over the baseline model when the target domain is out of the training data. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/pattern_aware_neural_reader.

Quantum computers are still largely incompatible with most implementations of the HHL algorithm, due in large part to the need to invert matrices on these devices, a task that can necessitate an inordinate amount of qubits and gates. Consequently, researchers and practitioners are developing modified versions of the HHL algorithm that are more suitable for the 'noisy-no noisless' quantum machines currently available. In our work, we introduce the NISQ- HHL algorithm, a variant of HHL that utilizes approximate matrix inversion and incorporates existing quantum amplitude amplification techniques to deliver efficient and accurate results on existing devices. By leveraging existing amplitude amplification templates and incorporating intermediate qubit reinitialization to prevent unnecessary qubit degradation, the NISQ-HHL algorithm excels particularly in applications where large-scale matrix inversion is unnecessary. Furthermore, the NISQ-HHL algorithm comes equipped with a scalable solution for managing qubit interconnectivity on these devices. Ours is the first reported variant of the HHL algorithm tailored specifically to the needs of near-term, noisy quantum machines. The NISQ-HHL algorithm has the added benefit of accommodating a broad spectrum of problem types, including linear systems with large condition numbers, in addition to providing an optimized execution that can be adjusted according to the capabilities of the device in question. In our testing, the NISQ-HHL algorithm demonstrated the capability to solve linear systems with massive matrices containing up to 800x800 entries for a wide range of condition numbers in a timely and accurate manner. We investigate how the $p$-norm used in a neural network affects its performance when optimizing a Lipschitz continuity constraint. Our investigation reveals that optimizing a $p$-norm-based Lipschitz constraint leads to a neural network that performs similarly to one optimized with the 2-norm-based Lipschitz constraint, despite requiring significantly more training time. To facilitate this investigation, we develop a method for constraining the Lipschitz continuity of a neural network using the $p$-norm, building on existing work related to the 2-norm-based Lipschitz constraint. Unlike previous studies, we do not assume that the neural network's weights follow a specific distribution; instead, we provide a theoretical analysis of how the $p$-norm-based Lipschitz constraint relates to the 2-norm-based version. We also offer empirical evidence showing that optimizing a $p$-norm-based Lipschitz constraint can be sensitive to hyperparameter choices. To make the method more practical, we simplify the $p$-norm-based Lipschitz constraint to obtain the 2-norm-based version's equivalent form. This form serves as the objective function for optimizing the neural network when the 2-norm-based Lipschitz constraint is used. To demonstrate the method's applicability, we train neural networks with both the 2-norm-based and $p$-norm-based Lipschitz constraints on three image classification tasks and a language translation task. In all cases, the trained networks perform similarly, despite being trained with more stringent Lipschitz constraints. This means that optimizing a 2-norm-based Lipschitz constraint is sufficient and helps generalize to both small and large transformation sizes. This finding holds true across different hyperparameter choices and when applying the method to recurrent neural networks. This research and the developed method are relevant to anyone interested in training neural networks with Lipschitz constraints, particularly when the focus is on robustness against adversarial attacks or improving model generalizability through regularization. This work's results and the introduced method are valuable for achieving robustness and generalizability in various machine learning applications involving neural networks. A deep-neural-network (DNN) approach was developed to enhance the quality of low-dose PET images using frame-by-frame training and the support of MRI images. The proposed DNN model consists of a U-Net based encoder--decoder structure that significantly reduces the number of required PET training data. To further improve image reconstruction results, the DNN was trained on a batch-by-batch basis using a coarse-grained descent algorithm. The effectiveness of this method was tested on 10 healthy subjects who underwent both PET and MRI scans. The assessment showed that DNN-reconstructed images from as few as 2-base PET data scans are comparable to those derived from 10-frame PET scans without DNN enhancement. Furthermore, the DNN method demonstrated comparable performance to conventional reconstruction techniques using 10-frame PET scans, but with significantly reduced scan times and corresponding decreased image noise. The assessed DNN-reconstructed images from 2-base PET scans also met clinical standards for various lesion metrics. The results with support from MRI images showed a higher success rate (100%) than without MRI images (90%) in meeting the aforementioned clinical standards. The proposed DNN-based approach has the potential to successfully translate research PET imaging techniques to clinical applications. A novel approach called single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling is proposed to generate multi-label data with superior quality and minimal labeling expenses. Initially, a model is trained to classify single-label data, and then the S2M sampling method is used to generate new samples that the model misclassifies. These negatively sampled examples are then labeled with the missing labels from the model's prediction. It is demonstrated that using these artificially generated labels as additional data enhances the model's performance. Experimental results show that using the S2M sampling method for negatively sampled data and positively sampled data yields different outcomes and requires different cutoff values for optimal performance. Further analysis reveals that using artificially generated positive labels as additional data leads to a significant improvement in performance, while using artificially generated negative labels as additional data results in a decrease in performance, although the difference lessens with increased dataset sizes. Additionally, the effectiveness of S2M sampling is validated across multiple large dataset scenarios, encompassing WebText and Wikipedia. This study proposes a novel deep neural network structure that detects cardiovascular diseases from noisy sound recordings based on a specific attention mechanism. Conventional sound classification networks struggle with noisy data, especially when classifying cardiovascular conditions from Doppler ultrasound recordings, which contain substantial spectral aliasing. To address this challenge, a deep neural network was developed, incorporating a channel attention mechanism in its frequency domain implementation. The attention mechanism's ability to ignore irrelevant spectral information enhances the network's robustness to noisy data. To evaluate the network's effectiveness, it was tested on a large dataset of recorded heart sounds with normal and stenotic conditions. The results show that the proposed network outperforms the conventional time and frequency domain approaches, including a well-known deep neural network, by achieving a 20.5% lower error rate in detecting stenotic conditions. Furthermore, the proposed network was found to be more resilient to noisy data and speckle interference, making it a suitable solution for real-world applications involving Doppler ultrasound recordings. The proposed network's superiority is demonstrated while using a relatively small number of training samples, indicating its potential for efficient cardiovascular disease detection across different populations. The proposed network's code has been made publicly available on GitHub, enabling the healthcare community to build upon this work for even better cardiovascular disease detection techniques. The challenge dataset used in this study is also publicly available on Figshare, enabling fair comparison with proposed methods in the future. The code and dataset can be accessed via the following links: https://github.com/2021-cmd-heart-sound-analysis (code) and https://figshare.com/projects/2021_Cardiac_Mechanical_Damage_Heart_SoundAnalysis_Challenge/41297 (dataset). The proposed network's performance can be improved by employing transfer learning and data augmentation techniques, such as mixing datasets and generating new samples through generative adversarial networks. The current proposal serves as a starting point for developing more advanced cardiovascular disease detection systems that are both accurate and robust in noisy environments. The attention mechanism proposed in this study can be applied to other classification problems involving non-stationary signals. The code and dataset available for this research contribute to the healthcare community's efforts to develop open and reproducible research practices, fostering fairness and building upon existing work for future innovation. Medical research institutions and organizations are increasingly facing data privacy challenges, threatening the scalability of health artificial intelligence systems.  To overcome this obstacle, a new federated learning approach called FedHealth has been developed to efficiently train activity recognition models using wearable devices.  Compared to standard methods, FedHealth significantly enhances accuracy on unseen data by combining model updates from various sources.  Initially designed for wearable activity recognition, this approach has the potential to be applied to other federated learning tasks involving mobile devices.  To facilitate widespread adoption, the FedHealth framework has been made open-source, enabling research institutions to seamlessly integrate it into their existing setups.  Future enhancements to the FedHealth platform will be announced on the project's website.  Experimental data shows that FedHealth yields a 13% boost in logistic regression accuracy and a 12% improvement in deep learning-based activity recognition, relative to traditional methods.  Additionally, it has been discovered that FedHealth exhibits reciprocal growth, benefiting from larger and more diverse datasets.  To further optimize the FedHealth algorithm, a novel selection approach has been proposed, where model updates are ranked according to their individual performance before being combined, resulting in a 25% improvement in accuracy over existing strategies.  The feasibility and effectiveness of FedHealth have been validated through comprehensive tests involving 13 subjects and covering 21 activities.  The associated code has been made available on the FedHealth repository at this link https://github.com/MITGH/FedHealth.  Future research directions for the FedHealth framework are discussed, paving the way for the development of a robust, unsupervised approach, as well as exploring ways to integrate temporal dynamics into the algorithm. The efficiency of an interview panel can be significantly enhanced by utilizing a scoring system and a progressive panel structure. These structures allow recruiters to rank candidates progressively across different panels, enabling them to focus on candidate details that are relevant to each panel. To achieve this efficiently, we need to schedule interviews and construct panels, tasks that involve minimizing the overall cost of transferring information between assessments. By leveraging existing solutions for the flow problem and grouping problems, we can develop algebraic descriptions and use them to create a hybrid algorithm for interview scheduling and panel creation. This hybrid algorithm utilizes a combination of fixed and variable parts to provide an optimal solution, and it serves as a basis for our hybrid algorithm that is further enhanced with clustering to tackle large-scale problems. We evaluate our hybrid algorithm in relation to other existing algorithms, including a random, a greedy, a hybrid of a maximum weight average, and a maximum weight matching algorithm. Our study indicates that the hybrid algorithm that we developed achieves the lowest cost when comparing with the other algorithms, an improvement of 25.6% over the best alternative algorithm. Additionally, our research reveals that our algorithm exhibits proportional relationships with respect to certain variables, such as the number of candidates, the number of panels, and the score base, demonstrating the scalability of our solution. We have implemented our algorithm, and the resulting code is available openly for other researchers to use, enabling them to schedule interviews and create panels more efficiently. This is particularly beneficial in high-stakes recruitment scenarios, such as hiring for aerospace engineering positions. Our study showcases a notable increase of 25.6% in panel efficiency that is achievable through the adoption of our algorithm, a performance gain that is equivalent to $250,000 per year if we apply it to the dataset of final candidates for aerospace engineering positions in Australia. This represents a significant amount that could be saved by companies and organizations through the optimized use of their current recruitment practices. We have made the code available openly so that other researchers can build upon our work, and we encourage them to do so in order to further improve our solution. We have conducted a thorough examination of our algorithm in relation to other existing algorithms through comprehensive tests, and the code we have developed can be utilized for interview scheduling and panel creation for any recruitment process that involves multiple stages, regardless of the industry in question. This research investigates an extended backward stochastic differential equation (BSEDD) that accounts for a underlying diffusion, denoted as the reference BSEDD, and provides a theoretical framework for solving a system of forward-backward SDEs with two components, known as the optimal payoff. We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the reference BSEDD and the two-component SDEs. Furthermore, we prove that the value of the optimal payoff can be expressed in terms of the solution to the reference BSEDD. Additionally, we establish the regularity of the solution to the two-component SDEs, which enables the identification of the optimal stopping time and the associated optimal payoff. This research was motivated by an extension of the problem first presented in the work of Gucong Li, where we build upon his results. We also touch on the numerically stable method for approximating the optimal payoff. This approach is based on a transformed form of the equation, which yields a higher order Euler scheme with a $4k$-order accuracy for a $k$-step approximation, where the accuracy is determined by the Euler scheme's order. This research was inspired by the high order Euler scheme presented in the work of Antonov and Nutz. We also explore the convergence analysis of this scheme. This approach provides a way to approximate the optimal payoff with a high order accuracy and offers a theoretical framework for solving a broader class of extended backward stochastic differential equations. The asymmetric production of leptoquark pairs in an electron-proton or a positron-proton collider has been overlooked in previous research. However, this process is feasible in the LHeC and future lepton-hadron colliders, offering promising insights into the properties of leptoquarks, particularly for heavy leptoquarks beyond the top quark. As our primary contribution, we detail the leptoquark pair production processes in these colliders, provide mathematical expressions for their cross-sections, and analyze these processes using a toy example. As our findings indicate, the asymmetric production process in these colliders can serve heavy leptoquark searches, with the relevant parameters influenced by the leptoquark type and the colliner component of leptoquarks. As an example, the cross-section for pair-producing heavy scalar leptoquarks in an electron-proton collider is directly proportional to the energy of the collider, in contrast to the quadratic relationship seen in conventional leptoquark pair production. Consequently, the LHeC or future lepton-hadron colliders can serve as complementary platforms for in-depth properties of heavy leptoquarks already discovered in future particle colliders. As our secondary contribution, we also explore the possibilities of leptoquark pair production in the asymmetric mode using existing particle colliders, discovering that certain leptoquark types are producible only in the 50 TeV future hadron lepton colliders. Additionally, we demonstrate that adding a heavy quark pair in the final state can significantly enhance the cross-section for leptoquark pair production in the asymmetric mode. Given the versatility of this process, we suggest it be considered in the research of leptoquarks in lepton-hadron deepfake colliders. Our analysis focuses on approximate analytic expressions for the power spectral density (PSD) of signals from individual relativistic binary sources and pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). We evaluated three approaches: (1) an analytical model based on a power series, (2) a description utilizing the usable frequency band's square root, and (3) an approximate analytic expression recently proposed. Through comparisons, we examined these methods' accuracy in relation to results from numerical integrations of relativistic orbits and pulse generation. For initial transients from inspiraling binaries, the power series and square root methods generally provided accurate approximations, especially in PTA frequency bands. However, for pulsars from GWB detections, these methods showed smaller corrections, offering simpler representations at the expense of minor precision loss. The recently proposed approximation showed comparable performance. We also explored the effects of pulse generation and timing model errors on PSD estimates. For most cases, deviations from the standard model remained within the approximate analytic ranges, except in the high-frequency bands of certain pulsars. Ultimately, we suggest that the approximate analytic expressions can effectively capture key features of PSD signals from individual sources in PTA experiments. These expressions, coupled with Monte Carlo simulations, may be used to model large binary populations' contributions to PSD signals. We also propose a statistical method to identify pulsars with detectable signals from individual binary sources. Given the sensitivity of PTA experiments, only the most massive binary sources will produce signals, primarily involving neutron stars in tight orbits. Nonetheless, even these elusive signals can be vital for understanding the physics of neutron star mergers, especially for millisecond pulsars. We estimate that a future PTA experiment could potentially detect about 100 such pulsars out of the million or so being monitored. Although most of these pulsars will be inaccessible for optical and gamma-ray observations, their mergers' progenitors will still be detectable by future wide-field infrared surveys, offering a direct link between PTA sources and massive binary mergers. Ultimately, the study of these sources within PTA experiments will provide a comprehensive picture of the relativistic binary population that gives rise to both primary and secondary gravitational wave sources. We have made the code utilized in our analysis an publicly accessible tool on GitHub, along with an example script for usage. The code utilizes the EOB numerical waveform model for inspiraling binaries, coupled with a timing model and a GW background model. We have also released the manuscript, along with supplementary materials, on a public repository. We have made an effort to maintain clarity in the paper

This research examines the ASEP system to explore the statistics of a third class of particles that can move through the system. All particles interact according to the standard ASEP rules, except for one specific type of particle – we'll refer to it as a star particle – which moves at a different speed than the others. To study the star particle's behavior, we create a modified ASEP system where the star particle is replaced by two particles of different classes that exchange positions with each other. This equivalent system allows us to study the star particle's statistics by examining two competing classes of particles. Our primary goal is to determine the average position of the star particle, denoted by the variable $M_n$, as a function of time. We demonstrate that the variable $M_n$ follows a specific probabilistic distribution characterized by a single parameter, which we determine to be $\mathrm{e}^{(2\theta-1)\tau}\big(1-\mathrm{e}^{-(2\theta-1)\tau}\big)/(2\theta-1)$. Additionally, we investigate the conditions under which the star particle's position becomes exponentially distributed as time progresses. We also consider a related system where the star particle moves at the same speed as the other particles, and in this case, its average position is directly proportional to time. Furthermore, we compare the shapes of velocity distributions for second-class particles in both the original ASEP system and the related system, and we observe that they both undergo the same gradual transformation over time, despite differing in shape. These comparisons also apply to the Eulerian fluid dynamics system, which is a more general version of ASEP. We further investigate the Eulerian fluid dynamics system with an additional feature – a third class of particles that can move through the system – and in this case, we are able to characterize the velocity distribution of second-class particles over time. We demonstrate that the associated probability distributions for both the ASEP system and the Eulerian fluid dynamics system converge uniformly to the same probability distribution as time progresses. We also consider a related system – the junction process – which shares similar characteristics with the Eulerian fluid dynamics system, and we are able to characterize the associated probability distributions for second-class particles over time. This research focuses on developing an optimization algorithm for fitting differential models to data from epidemiological studies, with a emphasis on ensuring the models' biological plausibility. Although differential models accurately capture the dynamics of various epidemiological phenomena, these models necessarily produce positive components that, when fitted to real data, may lead to feasibility issues. To address this challenge, we've created a method for minimizing the sum of squared errors between model predictions and actual data, subject to the models' positive constraints. Our approach uses a unique combination of the limited memory Broyden--Goldfarb--Shanno and quasi-Newton optimization algorithms. This model extends the conventional rigid pendulum approach, offering a deeper understanding of the system's dynamics and the onset of instability, and it does so without relying on the strength of the coupling. In our study, a specific parameter regime is examined where two stable states exist within the optical lattice, and the results are compared to existing rigid pendulum model predictions, revealing the limitations of the conventional approach. The effective non-rigid pendulum model is achieved through the application of a relevant rotation to the original Hamiltonian, and the corresponding parameters are mapped to the new framework, ensuring the legitimacy of the model. Our findings include the onset of beating dynamics, atom-molecule oscillations, and the formation of a stationary dark state, all of which are accurately described by the non-rigid pendulum model. The non-rigid pendulum model demonstrates a high degree of similarity to the actual system dynamics, demonstrating its effectiveness as a simplified yet representative model. Furthermore, this model offers valuable insights into the dynamics of related systems, including those with periodic driving forces, spatially separated atom-molecule interactions, and sudden quenches, and it provides a foundation for the development of more complex non-linear models. A key challenge in DNA data storage systems arises from the need to manage storage partitions effectively. This paper introduces a novel application of a centuries-old problem - the knights and horses problem - to efficiently handle partition planning. The proposed solution, called KHP-Primer, incorporates a precise strategy for creating and pairing DNA primers that enable precise retrieval of stored data. The design of primer pairs in KHP-Primer are systematically varied to conduct comprehensive research on different configurations and associated costs. The results show that the optimal solution, which minimizes storage costs while fulfilling primary requirements, can be difficult to determine manually. Consequently, the design of KHP-Primer is designed to be an automated tool that assists with primer design decisions based on varying priorities and constraints. The research on which KHP-Primer is based reveals that the knights and horses problem presents a suitable framework for exploring complex trade-offs in DNA data storage systems, offering valuable insights for their practical implementation. The KHP-Primer tool, along with the conducted experiments and an example of application to DNA data storage, is made publicly available on a designated website. Accurate riverbed bathymetry estimation is crucial for understanding and modeling the dynamics of rivers. A significant limitation in modeling river systems comes from measuring flow velocity rather than bathymetry directly. To address this challenge, a new geostatistical method called Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA) has been developed to interpret flow velocity data in a way that maintains spatial connectivity. By applying PCGA to a highly conductive riverbed with sandbanks, researchers successfully recovered bathymetry with results showing that PCGA yields equivalent results to traditional geostatistical approaches while providing a meaningful interpretation of unobserved variables. Furthermore, PCGA demonstrates robust performance even with limited flow velocity measurements, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. Source: Yeo, et al., 2023. The Madsen-Weiss theorem, a significant result in topology, was originally proven by the duo Andrew Madsen and Henrik Weiss. This theorem found an intriguing link between moduli spaces of genus $g$ surfaces with boundary and a specific topological concept called a Heegaard structure. In 2007, the theorem was re-proved by P. Teichmer and I. Hamenstaedt, and subsequently by S. Palmieri through a different approach. Given the significance of the Madsen-Weiss theorem within the realm of topological research, it is surprising to learn that until now, no attempt has been made to explore the underlying principles that the theorem embodies, specifically in relation to the recent applications of the B-principle. Our analysis indicated that CPM exceeds SPM by a factor of approximately twenty, leading us to suspect its dominance in the loop. We developed an alternative to the standard nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation that better models the interplay of CPM and SPM within the loop. This new equation assumes the same optical field structure for both propagation directions and includes both phase modulation terms. We numerically solved this new equation, obtaining results that compared with the alternative approach based on the standard nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with two different optical field structures for each propagation direction. While it yielded a more complex algebraic expression for the effective nonlinear coefficient, we found that the difference between them is marginal, likely because the loop resonator's short coherence time prevents the formation of a double optical soliton. Consequently, the effective nonlinear coefficient determines the loop's nonlinear behavior, allowing for a simplified model. We also validated our loop by generating an optical shockwave through the saturation of SPM and CPM. Ultimately, our simplified model provides a more efficient means of studying the nonlinear dynamics of loop resonators. We present a novel evaluation method that utilizes a dynamic curriculum to assess reinforcement learning algorithms. In this approach, a sequence of interconnected tasks is created, representing a gradual diffusion process. We then investigate how effectively various state-of-the-art reinforcement learning controllers adapt to these tasks as they progress through the curriculum. Our experiments on the underlying model demonstrate that it exhibits characteristics similar to real-world applications, involving a natural order of task dependencies. Furthermore, to enhance the validity of our results, we modified the environment to ensure that the curriculum diffusion process retains internal structure and coherence. Our findings reveal notable differences in the performance of reinforcement learning controllers, providing valuable insights into their strengths and limitations. Moreover, the dynamic nature of our evaluation allows for a more comprehensive understanding of controller performance, moving beyond traditional fixed test sets. Our research has implications for the development of reinforcement learning controllers in complex, real-world scenarios. Finally, we establish a connection between these components and certain subfields of the extension used to construct the cyclic cover. Neural machine translation has seen significant advancements in recent years, thanks in large part to the introduction of attention-based models and residual connections. Building on this progress, we have explored the potential applications of attention-based recurrent neural networks and fully neural networks in sentiment analysis and language translation. Our testing environment consisted of three datasets: a small, in-house dataset for sentiment analysis in Haitian Creole, and two larger datasets for Spanish to English translation. We discovered that our models were particularly effective in transferring knowledge and could be used for translation and sentiment analysis in languages other than the original training data. Specifically, we found that a model trained on Spanish to English translation could also be skilled to translate from English to Haitian Creole with only 0.12 million words of target text required for fine-tuning. Our model also achieved outstanding results in sentiment analysis on the Haitian Creole dataset with only 2% accuracy already achieved without fine-tuning. Our code is available online for others to build upon. Our approach has the potential to be a valuable tool for languages with limited resources by enabling the creation of high-performance models without the necessity of extensive amounts of local data. Our approach also highlights the potential of attention-based models to capture the essential structures and patterns of a language, allowing them to be effective in new languages with minimal adaptation. Our testing has shown that our model can be effective in new languages with minimal adaptation, however, more testing is necessary to determine the maximum extent to which our approach can be successful with more diverse sets of languages. This project aims to facilitate efficient distribution of limited healthcare resources in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) for COVID-19 patients by classifying patients based on their specific features upon ICU admission.  By classifying patients into three categories (requirement for mechanical ventilation, death, or recovery)  we can prioritize resource allocation accordingly.  To achieve this, we developed a multi-class decision tree model utilizing XGBoost, which effectively identified key features related to ICU admission.  Our results show that a simple decision-making approach, guided by the XGBoost model, can lead to better outcomes than a one-size-fits-all approach to ICU resource allocation.  To make this model practical for real-world application, we simplified the feature set while maintaining similar performance, indicating that a limited set of easily obtainable features upon ICU admission can be highly predictive of patient outcomes.  Consequently, this model can be utilized as a valuable tool to support healthcare professionals in making informed decisions about ICU resource allocation.  Furthermore, our analysis revealed specific features related to ICU admission that significantly influence patient outcomes, providing valuable insights for future treatment improvement.  To facilitate widespread adoption, we made the code and model publicly available, offering potential for customization to meet the needs of various healthcare settings.  Ultimately, our approach highlights the importance of considering the initial conditions of COVID-19 patients upon ICU admission when making resource allocation decisions. Visual Relationship Detection aims to identify relationships between objects within images by leveraging neural network models. The task is subject to various limitations, primarily stemming from the vast number of negative relationship candidates, making traditional sampling methods inefficient. To rectify this, we propose the Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling strategy, a data augmentation technique that reduces the sampling space by eliminating superfluous negative examples. By generating a set of supportive proposals for each region pair, BNPS enhances model performance through an optimized sample of negative relationships. We further introduce a novel decision tree-based approach to prioritize proposal pairs, refining the sampling process and delivering superior results compared to conventional methods. The proposed method demonstrates significant improvements in Visual Relationship Detection, surpassing current state-of-the-art results on the Visual Genome dataset. Fake news has been a significant concern on social media platforms, and detecting it relies heavily on machine learning.  Since the spread of false information is often intended to benefit financially or politically, creating and disseminating high-quality fake content poses an even greater threat.  Existing research has primarily focused on categorizing news articles as genuine or fabricated using text-based features, but it has not considered the underlying economics and propagation dynamics that give rise to fake news in the first place.  To address this limitation, we develop a novel, multi-agent model called MetaFEND that detects fake news by examining the mechanisms underlying its spread.  This model includes two agent populations with distinct behaviors in the MetaFEND dataset, which it identifies with automatic feature extraction, demonstrating a 14.5% higher detection accuracy than the current benchmark methods.  Furthermore, we discover that the most trustworthy sources are often susceptible to publishing fake news, and that the likelihood of doing so increases with their level of trust enjoyed in the community.  Ultimately, MetaFEND yields a 64.6% better performance than traditional machine learning methods and provides important insights that can be utilized to enhance the current anti-spread-fake-news initiatives.  The code for MetaFEND has been made publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zhongyuweizs/MetaFEND.  We also publish the MetaFEND dataset, which comprises 60,000 text samples and is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuweizs/MetaFEND-Dataset.  We strongly advise against using the following variables in the dataset as features for machine learning models: the actual text content.  Instead, we recommend utilizing the embedded numerical codes generated by the model, which are more effective in detecting fake news than the text itself.  We strongly encourage researchers to treat the following variables with caution: the trust enjoyed by the user and the source ID, which may constitute secondary targets for machine learning models due to their straightforward nature.  We recommend combining MetaFEND with existing methods that rely on text-based features for a more comprehensive detection of fake news. This paper investigates a one-dimensional transport equation with periodic conditions, where solutions can be expressed as integrals and the flux term involves a nonlocal operation, specifically the Hilbert transform. We consider an initial condition that starts from a smooth, odd function and shows that the solution will become unbounded in a finite amount of time if either the space period or the nonlocal integral coefficient is greater than 1. Furthermore, when both the space period and the coefficient are less than 1, we prove that the solution will eventually become infinite on each interval within its period. Our approach utilizes the energy estimate method. If the initial condition is not odd, we observe that the solution will also become unbounded due to its increasing gradient. We also demonstrate that when the nonlocal coefficient is greater than 1, the solution's norm will increase exponentially with time. In the case where the nonlocal coefficient is less than 1, we show that the solution will eventually become singular at each interval within its period, which we believe is reminiscent of a singularity similar to that found in the problem of formation of shock waves from a initial condition of the one-dimensional transport equation with nonlocal flux and no dissipation, also known as the Gelfand--Shilov problem. This research provides an initial exploration of this problem and raises several unanswered questions. We propose several possible future directions of study. This paper also presents an approach to modify the transport equation by adding a dissipation term, which prevents the solution from becoming unbounded. This approach allows us to study the solution's singularity more closely. We consider two approaches to adding a dissipation term: one is based on the use of the Maxwell--Boltzmann operator, which results in the addition of a Laplacian operator to the nonlocal flux, which we show can be interpreted as the combination of the Hilbert transform and the Maxwell--Boltzmann operator being equivalent to the combination of the nonlocal flux and the Laplacian operator; another approach is based on the use of the Maxwell--Boltzmann operator with a specific value, which we show can be interpreted as the combination of the Hilbert transform and a multiple of the Laplacian operator. Researchers are reaching for precise control over impurities' placement and the resulting quantum interactions in solid-state materials. Theoretical modeling suggests that in a silicon crystal, substitutional silicon dopants can be connected by a thin layer of single-photon emissions. We employ a quantum classic approach to investigate the impact of dopants placed in neighboring sites on the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction. By calculating the overlap of adjacent atoms' wavefunctions, we find that the exchange interaction varies significantly across the lattice, allowing for targeting of particular spin exchange frequencies across the spectrum. This variation can be manipulated through lattice strain, over 10-fold, and potentially, on-demand via optical pumping. A proposal for using 1.5 um laser lighting to prevent lossy blue-shift and maintain precise exchange interaction frequencies has been presented. Moreover, we demonstrate that the exchange interaction's energy range can be adjusted across the lattice, enabling for the construction of artificial spin networks through dopant placement. Ultimately, this regime of silicon quantum computing holds promise for both quantum simulation and artificial neural networks. The methodology introduced in this research extends to other group IV and III-V semiconductor materials. The theoretical exchange interaction energy predicted in this study positions silicon quantum computers for practical application in artificial neural networks and quantum simulation, while other materials may offer more extensive exchange interaction energy ranges. The silicon scenario, with the ability to adjust exchange interaction frequencies across the spectrum by placing the dopants, is deemed particularly appealing. The material's compatibility with CMOS technology, combined with the versatility of the exchange interaction frequency, makes silicon quantum computers suitable for artificial spin and boson systems, as well as zero-node neutral architectures. Developing accurate models of complex systems with probabilistic components is crucial for inferential techniques such as recovering a new system instance's underlying structure using observed time series data. Given the challenges associated with model learning from limited and noisy data, we propose a novel approach called STRIDE. STRIDE leverages a probabilistic neural process, combining a parametric model and a neural process to recover a latent distribution, enabling the inference of a new system instance's structure and parameters from observed time series data. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of STRIDE through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, showing its capabilities in recovering a target system's model, conducting Bayesian optimization, and performing conditionally dependent multi-step forecasting with a new system instance. Experimentally, STRIDE outperforms the baseline methods, namely, probabilistic neural processes and reinforcement learning, in recovering models and performing Bayesian optimization and, in some cases, matches the performance of state-of-the-art methods, such as neural state space models, in multi-step forecasting experiments. Additionally, we apply STRIDE to a real-world dataset related to port call scheduling, achieving a 13.4% improvement in overall system efficiency. The code for STRIDE is available on GitHub at https://github.com/QianHobbs/STRIDE.

A region of interest (ROI) is a confined section of an image that is analyzed independently by deep neural networks, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) play a significant role in imaging segmentation within these restricted areas. While the term "CNN-based feature extraction" is often used, the distinct contributions of CNNs in relation to fully convolutional networks (FCNs) for task-specific information have not been well-documented. Our proposed method, a 3D CNN used for extracellular matrix (ECM) segmentation within ROI in cardiac magnetic resonance images, is the subject of our analysis. By employing a multi-resolution approach and integrating a patch-based strategy, our model demonstrates superior performance compared to existing solutions. The depthwise separable convolution technique can be applied to CNNs to achieve a notable improvement in efficiency with only a minimal decline in accuracy. Our research provides a comprehensive evaluation of the model's performance in multiple aspects and highlights the potential advantages of a cascaded approach that combines CNNs and FCNs for ECM segmentation. This is especially evident when the model is trained to segment the entire image from scratch. Our results show that a focused analysis of CNN contributions within ROI segmentation aligns with the principles of efficient deep learning, particularly when imaging data is limited. Our research provides a foundation for further innovation in cardiac ECM segmentation and suggests that the 3D CNN model we developed is a viable solution that is both effective and efficient. GP2 introduced a significant enhancement to its data structure, replacing List with BigArray, and observed a marked improvement in the execution speed of graph-oriented programs. However, a slowdown in program performance remained unchanged at 3 orders of magnitude behind native compilation, likely due to the overhead of functional operations. In response to this challenge, we developed a linearized version of BigArray, dubbed LinearArray, and successfully applied it to array-oriented programs in GP2, resulting in a 4.5 times speed boost and reducing memory usage by half. Furthermore, by further simplifying LinearArray, we created ImmArray, which exhibited equivalent performance when using additional explicit memory pointers, thus paving the way for future optimizations. The actual implementation of ImmArray was too complex for GP2 and necessitated a more fundamental change to its core, thereby presenting an intriguing research question for the GP2 community. The underlying idea of simplifying data structures through linearization can be applied to other general-purpose virtual machines, offering a versatile solution, and we believe it presents a worthwhile investigation for the GP2 development team and a valuable contribution to the GP2 research ecosystem. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that enhances the appearance of fonts by accurately rendering line joins. Unlike conventional techniques, the proposed method correctly reproduces the precise shapes of line joins, particularly the pointed ends of lines, even when rendered at high magnifications. Due to the inherent limitations of scalarization, traditional halo rendering methods fail to accurately depict the peaked ends of line joins, resulting in subpar font rendering, particularly in vector graphics displays. To address this issue, the proposed algorithm generates a vector halo around the specified line join area and employs a sophisticated distance estimation technique to determine the appropriate scale for rendering. Moreover, the proposed method leverages the existing halo functionality to render the desired line joins smoothly. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a sample font rendering application, and the benefits of line join halo rendering are illustrated through a real-world example of a font rendered with both the proposed and traditional methods. The proposed algorithm's advantages are also highlighted through a performance evaluation. The proposed algorithm's source code is available for public use on GitHub. A novel speech enhancement method known as the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) is proposed, consisting of a Convolution Recurrent Network (CRN) component with two distinct pathways for frequency and temporal details, respectively. The frequency pathway utilizes a convolution recurrent structure to successfully capture high-frequency spectral information. In contrast, the temporal pathway employs a simple recurrent cell to effectively handle time-domain information and previously generated spectral details. The effectiveness of DPCRN is demonstrated by achieving the lowest PESQ score of 3.302 in a real-time speech enhancement task, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods including DACRNs and DACRNs-Big with significant margins of 11.6% and 13.3% respectively. Additionally, DPCRN demonstrates superior performance in removing various types of background noise, including both clean and music-based environments. The source code of DPCRN has been made publicly available on GitHub at the address: https://github.com/zhengyunyang/DPCRN-SPEECH-ENHANCEMENT. The proposed network has shown significant enhancements in speech quality without the need for post-processing, as evidenced by PESQ and STOI score results of 3.302 and 1.119, respectively. The code has been released to facilitate further research in speech enhancement using time-frequency domains. The proposed DPCRN model has been found to be highly effective in enhancing noisy speeches with various levels of background noise. The model has been tested on a dataset with 6 different noise types, including the following: metraloud, coffee shop, guitar, babble, airplane and white noise, and showed superior performance in all cases. The model has also been evaluated on a more challenging condition with lower PESQ score of 2.5 and showed significant improvement of 21.8% over the current state-of-the-art method DACRNs. The proposed DPCRN model has been found to be compatible with real-time speech enhancement tasks due to its relatively small model size of 1.4 million parameters, which enables it to be used in scenarios with strict time and memory constraints. The time domain speech information is maintained through a simple recurrent cell within the CRN component, which facilitates the model's real-time capability. The proposed DPCRN model has been compared with current state-of-the-art methods including DACRNs and DACRNs-Big with model sizes of 5.9 million and 21.0 million parameters, respectively. A basic two-fluid model is proposed to analyze the dynamics of convective flows in a temperature gradient, specifically in Rayleigh-B\'enard convection. The model assumes a smooth interface between two fluid layers of significantly different temperatures and flows, and it is found that the model mimics the behavior of the Navier-Stolz equations even when the interface is turbulent, as long as the temperature difference is sufficiently large. By simplifying the model, a linear dynamics model is created for the fluid interface, which shows that the interface can be either stable or exhibit periodic oscillations. If the interface is unstable, the heat transferred from the lower layer to the upper layer is significantly higher than expected. A scaling rule for heat transfer is derived from the two-fluid model, which matches the findings of previous laboratory studies. Moreover, the two-fluid model predicts that the heat transfer will increase with an order of magnitude for each order of magnitude change in the temperature difference, which is similar to the findings of previous studies on the self-similar temperature distributions along the interface. The model also predicts that the interface oscillation frequency is directly proportional to the square root of the temperature difference, which is similar to the findings of previous studies on the interface dynamics. Nonetheless, the model needs further development to better match the dynamics of the interface, which includes the formation of cells in the upper layer. The model needs a larger dynamic range to model the interface dynamics for smaller temperature differences. The model can be used to design convective flows with optimized heat transfer rates. The model shows that the heat transfer rate can be increased by at least an order of magnitude for the same setup by increasing the temperature difference. The model also shows that the interface dynamics are sensitive to the surface roughness of the lower layer, which can affect the performance of heat exchangers in industrial applications. The model predicts that the interface dynamics will become less stable when the surface roughness of the lower layer increases above a certain threshold, which is similar to the findings of previous studies on the interface dynamics in convective flows. The model needs further development to better match the dynamics of the interface for larger temperature differences, which includes the formation of cells in the upper layer and the formation of thermal convection in the upper layer. The model can be used to design convective flows with optimized heat transfer rates and interface dynamics for different temperature differences. The model shows that the interface dynamics can be made more stable by increasing the surface roughness of the lower layer, which can affect the performance of heat exchangers in industrial applications

We investigate the generation of multipartite entanglement among atoms in a cavity system, incorporating both classical and quantum communications. A single cavity is connected to two channels: one leading to an unentangled atom that interacts with the cavity, and the other to a previous pair of entangled atoms within the cavity. As the unentangled atom interacts with the cavity, it becomes entangled with the cavity's field, which in turn becomes entangled with the initial pair of atoms. We examine the development of three-atom entanglement in two different scenarios: one initiated by a two-atom system and the other initiated by a single atom. In both cases, the distribution of entanglement slope among the atoms varies with the duration of interaction. Notably, the most distant atom from the unentangled pair generally exhibits the most significant increase in entanglement, and we have established an analytical formula for its entanglement slope. Additionally, the distribution of entanglement among the atoms can be influenced by the duration of interaction in both scenarios. We have further established conditions under which the entanglement distribution becomes uniformly balanced among the atoms. Lastly, the potential applications of this generation method are discussed. This approach presents a promising, experimentally feasible technique for creating multipartite entanglement among distant atoms utilizing cavity-based communication systems. The study at hand provides a comprehensive understanding of the intricate dynamics of cavity-based entanglement generation, offering a valuable foundation for various quantum technology developments, including quantum memories, quantum simulators, and universal quantum computers. The findings can be extended to include both discrete and continuous frequency spaces, and the corresponding parameters can be adjusted accordingly. Social media feedback monitoring relies heavily on processing large amounts of text data. Deep learning techniques have proven to be highly effective in this context, despite the difficulty in gaining insight into their decision-making processes. We believe that by simplifying deep learning models, their transparency and explanatory power can be enhanced, thereby providing a foundation for future CRFT development. In this study, a linear regression-based long short-term memory (LSTM) network is proposed, resulting in a model that exhibits superior performance, increased transparency, and lower concept shift risk compared to conventional LSTM models. The efficacy of this new model is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on two sensitive text classification tasks: sentiment analysis of tweets and online hotel reviews. Experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approaches, including conventional LSTM models, tree-based models, and word-level embedding-based models. Furthermore, an analysis of the model's parameters and component importance provides valuable insights into its internal decision-making processes, allowing for potential applications in automated parameter tuning and feature selection. This research investigates how the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter affects black holes in an asymptotically anti-de Sitter space-time. By examining a specific model where non-linear electrodynamics combines with a Yang-Mills field, we found that the parameter does not just alter the black hole's temperature but also leads to a deviation from the conventional power-law behavior observed in certain non-linear electrodynamics theories. Furthermore, the shadow radius and thermal profile of the black hole also change under the influence of this parameter. Notably, a critical value exists where the shadow radius reaches a minimum before increasing again. The analysis involves detailed calculations of thermodynamic quantities and the superconducting holographic duality, where the appearance of a gap in the quark density is explained by the change in the thermal profile. The effects of this parameter are observable in the infrared region of the Quark-Gluon Plasma. The associated radius of the shadow can serve as an important observable in gravitational wave physics. This study introduces a novel method to analyze the evolution of optical tomograms, focusing on Mach-Zehnder interferometer systems. By utilizing the Wigner function representation, we can observe nonclassical phenomena such as entanglement dynamics and entropic growth. We demonstrate how our approach leads to an accurate description of continuous wave optical parametric amplification, including its initial state, evolution, and measurement outcomes. Furthermore, we compare our method to other approaches, including the Husimi-Q function and Weyl-Wigner representations, and demonstrate that it yields a non-negative f-function for classical and positive $f$-functions for nonclassical states. Additionally, we investigate the scalability of our method for increasing photon populations and present applications for experimental reconstruction of optical states. This approach has been validated through simulation of actual experimental data, and the associated code is available online for modification and use with other systems. The theory of decoupling for linear systems with small perturbations relies on two analytical techniques: Taylor series expansion and the study of canonical surfaces. We combine these approaches to analyze the dynamics of decoupling, using Taylor series to examine the decoupling process near a fixed point of a system, and the study of canonical surfaces to determine the conditions under which a system exhibits the desired behavior for the decoupling property. We also establish sufficient conditions for the decoupling property to hold, which involve the system's parameters, the size of the perturbation, and the duration for which the system meets certain criteria. By integrating the findings from Taylor series expansion and the study of canonical surfaces, we provide an illustrative application to a specific system. We also offer a modified analysis that eliminates the requirement for the study of canonical surfaces. Finally, we discuss the implications of our research for the property of recurrence, which is a key aspect of many systems. We conclude by highlighting the potential applications of our research to a broad range of linear systems with small perturbations, including those found in biology, chemistry, climate studies, and medical studies. We also explore the property of recurrence in relation to the decoupling property. We demonstrate how our research can be applied to a specific system - the dynamics of a single species in epidemiology - and examine the conditions under which this system meets the decoupling property, in addition to the property of recurrence. The role of renormalization and counter-renalization in the color dipole gluon distribution is being closely examined, particularly in relation to uncertainty quantification. However, the impact of counter-renalization, specifically in the $N^k$ counter-renalization, is currently unknown and is believed to be insignificant. A study has been conducted to determine the effect of $N^k$ counter-renalization on the color dipole gluon distribution at a next-to-next-to-leading order, particularly in relation to hadron collisions. It was found that counter-renalization counteracts the impact of infrared renormalons on the gluon distribution, potentially influencing the estimated uncertainty. A estimation of the counter-renalization's impact on the estimated uncertainty of the gluon distribution at a next-to-leading order is also proposed. Additionally, the study highlights some peculiar characteristics of $N^k$ counter-renalization in QCD. The study's findings are relevant to recent studies on the gluon distribution's uncertainty, particularly in relation to jet production in hadron collisions. It is also worth noting that the issue of counter-renalization's impact is not unique to the color dipole gluon distribution, but rather a broader problem affecting all hadron parton distributions at higher orders. A possible approach to address this problem involves restricting the counter-renalization to a level that minimizes the impact of infrared renormalons on the gluon distribution, thereby reducing the estimated uncertainty. This research demonstrates that the estimated uncertainty of the gluon distribution at a next-to-next-to-leading order can be decreased by approximately a factor of two in jet multiplicity studies, and the effects of different counter-renalization prescriptions on the gluon distribution's uncertainty can be distinguished in sub-jet studies. It is further suggested that the issue of counter-renalization may be alleviated to some extent by utilizing a better-defined gluon distribution, one that is less affected by the problems associated with counter-renalization, and which can be obtained through the utilization of better-defined counter-renalization, i.e. collinear and infrared-safe counter-renalization. It is also proposed that such a gluon distribution could serve as a higher-order correction to the color dipole gluon distribution at a next-to-next-to-leading order, rather than being used to describe hadron collisions directly. It is also worth noting that the research raises some important questions regarding the impact of counter-renalization on other hadron parton distributions at higher orders, and its related uncertainty

The presence of a Rayleigh anomaly edge in the reflectivity spectra allowed us to identify the surface plasmon-Rayleigh anomaly coupling, which intensified the magneto-optical effects by creating a resonance with a long decay length along the crystal. However, this coupling also led to a decay of the surface plasmon mode, which we observed as a minimum in the reflectivity spectra. The magnitude of this minimum varied significantly depending on the wavelength, which we attributed to the variation of the surface plasmon wavelength along the crystal. Notably, the magnitude of this maximum increased with the angle of incidence, which we linked to the orientation of the surface plasmons and the magnetophotonic crystal layers. Knowledge distillation is a significant technique for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic a high-capacity network. The traditional approach requires access to the high-capacity network's output, which can be impractical for certain applications where only the network's input and output are available. In such cases, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3) can be employed, where the compact model is trained to mimic the same decisions as the original network. In this research, an enhanced DB3 method is developed and several significant observations are made about current approaches and algorithms. Specifically, the proposed method leverages the distillation of a proxy network from the original network, achieves improved performance, and provides a clear structure for future DB3 techniques. Additionally, our results demonstrate significant improvements in our proposed methods across multiple scenarios. Our DB3 technique is tailored for instances where only the input and output of the original network are accessible, demonstrating substantial advantages over traditional knowledge distillation. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub, and our approaches can be applied to various tasks and networks. Furthermore, our findings hold value for future DB3 research and provide a useful framework for various black-box knowledge distillation scenarios. Our team has also published related work on database-based black-box knowledge distillation, which involves training a compact model using a dataset generated by the original network, and has been accepted for publication at the 2023 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). Our research has been financially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Science and Technology Planning Project of Guangdong Province. Our team also appreciates the valuable feedback provided by Dr. Wei Wei and Dr. Han Huang. Our proposed method has been tested on various datasets, including the CIFAR-10, Tiny-IMAGENET, and Wildlife datasets, and has shown significant improvements over current state-of-the-art approaches, especially in situations with limited data. Our team has also published related work on knowledge distillation, which involves transferring knowledge from a high-capacity network to a compact model, and has been widely applied in various machine learning scenarios, including but not limited to, deep neural networks, reinforcement learning, and probabilistic models. An analysis of $B$ meson decays into two neutral $K$ mesons is performed using 349 inverse femtobarns of data from $pp$ collisions at 13 TeV, collected with the CMS detector at the LHC. Decays of interest involve $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ decays that occur via two pathways: $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\eta(958)$ followed by $\eta(958)\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$, and $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\phi\rightarrow J/\psi \mu^+\mu^+\mu^-\mu^-$. By calculating branching fractions for these processes, uncertainties associated with them are also determined. Further, an upper limit on the branching fraction for $B_d^0\rightarrow J/\psi\eta(958)\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^+$ decay is established. Calculated branching fractions are 1.83 $± 0.21$ for the $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\eta(958)$ decay and 5.38 $± 0.70$ for the $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\phi\rightarrow J/\psi \mu^+\mu^+\mu^-\mu^-$ decay. Additionally, an upper limit of 4.30 is set for the $B_d^0\rightarrow J/\psi\eta(958)\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^+$ branching fraction. These measurements are in line with previous findings and forecasts. In the Standard Model, the $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\eta(958)$ process primarily occurs via the electroweak box diagram, making the branching fraction for this process sensitive to $|V_{ts}|^2$. As such, the measurement of $|V_{ts}|^2$ is updated to be (3.69 ± 0.23) × 10^-3. The analysis also examines the $B_s^0\rightarrow J/\psi\phi\rightarrow J/\psi \mu^+\mu^+\mu^-\mu^-$ decay mode in two scenarios: within the Standard Model, where the process is primarily driven by the weak phase, and in scenarios with modified CKM matrix, such as the one with minimal flavor violation, where the process is largely governed by strong interactions rather than weak interactions.
