Given a solvable group G and a multiplicity-free module M, we establish the compatibility of the composition factor array with the submodule lattice's structure for any of its submodules Δ(M). As a result, we can recover the original composition factor array from Δ(M) by using this compatible structure. We achieve this understanding by effectively redefining the composition factor array at each conjugacy class of irreducible non-trivial constituents of M, taking into account the occurrence frequencies. Consequently, we gain insight into how the original composition factor array can be reconstructed from the information contained within the lattice of submodules Δ(M). Moreover, our investigation leads to a straightforward algorithm for computing the frequency distributions of these classes and providing a detailed illustration through an illustrative example. We also clarify the distinction between composition factor arrays that are considered equivalent and those that are not, and in the process, we discover the inherent connection between the composition factor array and the distribution of irreducible constituents across the lattice of submodules Δ(M), giving rise to what we term the "composition sieve" that is derived from its underlying structure. Ultimately, our study lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive exploration into the intricate relationships between the lattice structures of submodules, module composition factors, and the associated group theory. We hope that our research will spark an examination into the universal properties that these structures exhibit, going beyond the specific example of solvable groups, to the more general case of arbitrary groups. In the process, we establish the basis for a theoretical framework that enables us to recompose the original module M from its submodules and composition factor array, thereby demonstrating the inherent stability of this module reconstruction process. Furthermore, we discover that this reconstruction process results in a module that is computationally isomorphic to the original module M. We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a novel framework that enables agents to acquire expertise in multiple tasks with different difficulty levels by working together. This approach leverages an innovative two-layer architecture, comprising an easy network that generates informative features, which are then used by multiple hard networks, one for each task. The agent's training involves minimizing the difference between the predicted actions for the easy network and the corresponding hard network, using a theoretically derived coefficient. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Co-Imitation Learning by applying it to challenging control problems, including a challenging pendulum scenario and a challenging spring mass damping problem, with results showing substantial performance gains compared to traditional imitation learning methods. Additionally, our framework facilitates efficient deployment, as generating the feature network is significantly less computationally intensive than training each hard network individually. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenyuXu90/Co-ImitationLearning.

This research investigates how different bias values in the polarized cutoff rate affect a sequential decoder's performance. A systematic approach has been developed to analyze the conditions under which a decoder using a uniformly set cutoff rate makes mistakes. Additionally, the study examines two scenarios where the decoder uses a incorrectly set cutoff rate due to either random error or intentional manipulation of the cutoff rate. A random bias leads to an inaccurate decoder, whereas a biased bias can result in the decoder either consistently producing more errors or never making any. The study also considers intentional biases by different entities and shows that a decoder using a certain cutoff rate will produce the maximum number of errors at a specific point at the beginning of the sequence. The research further explores the minimum number of bits required to ensure a decoder makes exactly one mistake, as this number relates to the sequence's starting point, bias, and cutoff level. The relationship between the minimum number of bits, the cutoff level, and the sequence's initial part is analyzed in depth. The study establishes a threshold for the polarized cutoff rate, below which a decoder will consistently produce more errors, and also establishes another threshold for a specific scenario in which the decoder will always make exactly one error. The relationship between these two thresholds is examined in depth. The research on random and intentional biases by different entities provides insights into the decoder's performance and offers a foundation for exploring more complex scenarios. The study's results for different bias scenarios have been validated through simulation using the GZIP compressed binary sequence as an example. The investigation reveals that the condition under which a decoder produces the maximum number of errors occurs most quickly at the beginning of the sequence, and the research provides a more detailed understanding of the decoder's performance in this scenario. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of reliable communication systems that can prevent sequential decoder failures due to improper cutoff rate settings. The study's results for different bias scenarios may also guide the development of secure communication systems that can prevent sequential decoder failures due to intentional manipulation of the cutoff rate by malicious entities. Using reinforcement learning, a value function is proposed to guide the generation of machine translation outputs. Previous studies have focused on optimizing the policy, but the present research reveals that reinforcing the value function yields superior performance. A key discovery of this work is that the value function's effectiveness can be enhanced by optimizing the action space, which leads to significant improvements in evaluation metrics. A novel training regime with agent-augmented learning is introduced, and the findings show that optimizing the value function outperforms a baseline model that is 10 points higher in BLEU score after re-ranking. Additionally, the proposed method achieves results 3 points better than standard reinforcement learning in certain settings. A significant observation made here is that the value function's action-dependent aspect aids in capturing semantic aspects like tone and register, which are difficult to model using conventional statistical methods. The proposed agent-augmented learning technique presents potential future directions for reinforcing value functions during generative tasks. The present research uses a simple value function design, but the underlying idea is valuable and can be applied to more intricate models using different value function architectures. The proposed method can be applied to other reinforcement learning-based machine translation genres, such as controlled generation and micro-fusion. The evaluation protocols used in this research are predictable evaluation and human assessment, which focus on evaluating the translation's grammaticality and tone/register, respectively. The associated data and code for this research are available online. The proposed agent-augmented learning technique provides a novel perspective on reinforcing value functions during generative tasks and offers implications for future research in this area. The present research reveals that optimizing the action space is crucial for improving the performance of reinforcement learning models in machine translation tasks, which is confirmed under different value function designs and various evaluation criteria. The findings shown here can be applied to other controlled generation tasks that involve evaluating the convergence of actions generated by reinforcement learning models. The associated code and data for this research are available online at the following repository: https://github.com/Qianhui Liu/Reinforcing Value Functions in Machine Translation. The current version of this research is v2, which was previously known as Study on Reinforced Value Function-Based Machine Translation. Quantum information flow between an open system and its surroundings can move in both directions, as demonstrated using a single-photon cutter system. When interacting with the system, the cutter can send quantum information to the environment, and subsequently, the environment can transmit the same quantum information back to the system. This two-way information transfer is made possible by utilizing a rare-earth ion as the system, coupled to a cavity which is then connected to a cavity with the environment. The system's ability to process quantum information is verified through the creation of a Bell-state, while the information's accuracy is tested by measuring the two-way information transfer's accuracy at various cutter-environment distances. Furthermore, the cutter can maintain the quantum information for up to 1.5 milliseconds, as the absence of direct sender-receiver interaction prevents information decay. This achievement highlights the potential for cutter-based ensembles to facilitate two-way information transmission between open systems and their environment. This phenomenon's potential applications include generating quantum distributions, conducting Bell-test experiments, and implementing quantum protocols for multiple parties. This breakthrough also paves the way for exploring rare-earth-based cutter ensembles in both classical and quantum settings. First, it is demonstrated that in order for a hypersurface to be minimal, certain conditions must be met when the hypersurface is subject to specific curvature restrictions in the Euclidean space. 

Next, it is shown that when the hypersurface is subject to these curvature restrictions in the Euclidean space, it will always be minimal if it satisfies one of the following conditions: it is harmonic, it has harmonic gauge, or it has harmonic mean curvature. 

Finally, it is demonstrated that when the hypersurface is not necessarily harmonic, it can still be considered minimal if it satisfies one of the following conditions: it has a specific relation between its mean curvature and a particular operator in a Euclidean space, or it has a particular operator equal to zero in a Euclidean space. 

This research paper also explores and identifies several examples of biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space that do not meet the required condition for minimality. 

Furthermore, it is demonstrated that in the Euclidean space, the condition for a hypersurface to be minimal is more stringent than the condition required for it to be stable.

This study examines the concurrency control mechanisms of three widely used, open deployments of MongoDB: WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER. Our analysis reveals that these deployments adhere to specific versions of snapshot isolation, including strict snapshot isolation, semi-strong snapshot isolation, and easy snapshot isolation. Our investigation into the underlying mechanisms of these deployments provides valuable insights into their behavior, revealing both anticipated and unforeseen consequences of their implementation. Furthermore, our findings highlight potential vulnerabilities to certain phenomena, such as stale read, false shutdown, and non-atomic multi-client interactions. Our research also explores potential improvements to these deployments, including alternative concurrency control strategies and additional safety guarantees. Our study's contributions are threefold, offering a comprehensive understanding of current deployments, identifying areas for improvement, and establishing a foundation for further exploration into concurrent database transactions. Our research demonstrates that the complexity of snapshot isolation in distributed databases surpasses the simplicity of their formal definitions, emphasizing the importance of a nuanced, empirically driven analysis of these systems. Our studies' results and methodologies are made available through an accompanying repository, allowing for the replication of our research and its extension beyond the scope examined here. Our findings also highlight the critical need for more rigorous, empirically grounded evaluations of distributed database concurrency control mechanisms, reflecting the significant gap currently existing in the field. Our research toward filling this gap is intended to benefit the large community of database users, developers, and researchers, empowering them with a more precise understanding of the reliability of distributed databases constructed from scalable, distributed data management systems. Our research's empirical approach is unusual within the database concurrency control domain, which is primarily characterized by theoretical research, illustrating the unique nature of our contribution. Ultimately, our studies aim to contribute to the development of more trustworthy and concurrently accessible distributed databases, showcasing the potential of a detailed, empirical examination of the interplay between concurrency control, transactions, and system scalability. Our exploration of MongoDB's deployments also uncovered several overlooked topics in the field, such as the interplay between concurrency control and flash storage or the atomicity of transactions across geographically dispersed locations, indicating a substantial unmet need for future research. Our study's limitations are two-fold, reflecting the challenges of analyzing complex, distributed systems as well as the constraints of a one-year research period, during which we could only examine a limited set of database deployments, uncover their underlying mechanisms, and explore the space of possible research beyond what we have shared here. Our empirical approach is designed to be easily replicable, allowing other researchers to build upon our findings

We demonstrate that the $e$-positive properties of chromatic symmetric functions can be characterized via restrictions on Dyck paths, showing that each of these functions corresponds to a specific subset of Dyck paths that are both above the path of weights and have a certain "depth" condition. This characterization serves as the foundation for developing an algorithm to compute the key $e$-positive invariant of these functions, referred to as the depth sequence. This depth sequence itself possesses $e$-positive properties and can be computed from a variety of alternative sources. By examining the relationship between the depth sequence and the classical Eulerian numbers, we also derive a combinatorial interpretation for the latter. Furthermore, our analysis enables us to determine the boundaries of which the $e$-positive functions, defined by Miller and Stumbo, can be mapped to the context of chromatic symmetric functions. This, in turn, facilitates an enhancement to their result, extending it to a broader class of polynomials known as the bi-$e$-positive functions. This achievement represents an expansion of the $e$-positive domain, which we illustrate through the instance of Egecioglu-Remmel functions. By demonstrating that these latter functions are both bi-$e$-positive and have connections to lattice paths, we are able to establish a more intricate relationship between the depth sequence and these bi-$e$-positive properties, allowing us to develop a novel formula that defines them. This formula itself can be interpreted through the lens of refined Eulerian numbers. Moreover, our research on the bi-$e$-positive properties of the depth sequence enables us to derive multiple cumulative sum and difference formulas, which are tied to various strategic placement problems, thereby providing a combinatorial framework for understanding these bi-$e$-positive properties. This framework is specifically tailored towards understanding the particular bi-$e$-positive properties of the classical Eulerian numbers, which form the foundation of numerous strategic placement problems, including those that involve optimal positioning within lattice structures, as well as other bi-strategic placement problems as noted in the subsequent sections. Finally, our bi-$e$-positive property formulas can be applied to evaluate the bi-$e$-positive invariants of the depth sequence for various specific instances, which are thereby shown to be both bi-strategically placed and satisfy the requirements of optimal positioning within lattice structures. We investigated the dynamic behavior of Ising spins arranged in a specific geometric configuration - each spin is connected to three neighbors, forming a triangle. This model can be used to simulate a fully connected random network, exhibiting a first-order phase transition when subject to an external magnetic field. By studying the hysteresis loop formed during cyclic applications of the magnetic field, we found that the loop transforms from a sharp corner to a smooth curve. The corner's sharpness, however, reappears at low temperatures, revealing the complex interplay of low-energy excitations and the surrounding energy landscape. The loop's shape also changes from symmetric to asymmetric as the temperature increases, mirroring the entropic characteristics of the energy landscape. The reduction of asymmetry at high temperatures is further influenced by central peak dynamics, which were discovered through deep elastic neutron scattering simulations. The impact of elastic fluctuations on the hysteresis loop's shape can be modulated by changing the spin-spin interaction strength, offering a feasible experimental setup to investigate the energy landscape's entropic properties through magnetic hysteresis analysis. The research reveals that the complex geometry of interacting spins can result in a range of outcomes, including the stabilization of polarized spins at high temperatures, as well as the coexistence of spin populations with different temperatures, which can be tuned by adjusting the interaction strength. The energy distributions of the interacting spins were found to follow power-law characteristics, transforming from a fat-tailed distribution to a Gaussian distribution with increasing temperature. The underlying energy landscape's long-tailed characteristics, however, persist up to the highest temperatures studied, suggesting that the concept of energy scale incompatibility is relevant across all interacting spin systems examined. The research provides a thorough understanding of the dynamic hysteresis behavior in interacting spins within a specific geometric configuration, uncovering the complex interplay of low-energy excitations and the surrounding energy landscape, as well as the entropic characteristics of the energy landscape itself. The findings offer a feasible experimental setup to investigate the energy landscape's entropic properties through magnetic hysteresis analysis. The study also reveals the coexistence of spin populations with different temperatures, as well as power-law distributions of energy fluctuations among interacting spins, which can be tuned by adjusting the interaction strength. The relevance of the research is demonstrated through realistic simulations of a fully connected random network, exhibiting a first-order phase transition when subject to an external magnetic field. Recent observations near the Sun reveal a fascinating phenomenon: where the solar wind is intense, a significant amount of energy is required to overcome solar gravitation, particularly at small distances. Conversely, regions with weaker winds require less energy. By examining data from six missions, we found that the distribution of energy needed to navigate the inner solar system mirrors the pattern of solar wind intensity, with 90% of all readings falling within the range of Earth's magnetic field influence. Notably, the most extreme readings, needing more energy to reach a particular speed, are extremely rare at 1 AU, but become more common at heliocentric distances between 0.6 and 0.8 AU. Moreover, the energy needed to reach a certain speed also varies significantly with the time of year, with the lowest readings occurring during solstices and the highest during equinoxes. The most energetic readings are found in regions with strong solar winds, specifically in areas where intense storms are present, and these readings can need up to ten times more energy to reach a particular speed than the least energetic readings. The relationship between energy needed and heliocentric distance is more complex, with a sharp increase in energy needed at distances less than 0.5 AU, but the main factor remains the variation in solar wind intensity rather than the distance itself. The variation in energy needed also impacts spacecraft, with the potential for more frequent communications, the ability to operate in certain regions, and the possibility of reducing costs associated with navigating the inner solar system. Furthermore, the data suggests that the energy needed to reach a certain speed in the inner solar system follows a power law distribution, with specific parameters depending on the location and time of year. The energy needed to reach a particular speed in the inner solar system can be predicted with an accuracy of 90% by considering just two factors: the average wind speed and the distance from the Sun, with a 30% reduction in error when considering additional factors. The knowledge gained from this research is valuable for planning space missions, particularly those involving close approaches to the Sun, and highlights the importance of considering the variation in solar wind speed and its impact on the energy needed to navigate the inner solar system. The most significant outcome of this study is a solar wind map, with the energy needed to reach a particular speed in the inner solar system mapped for the first time, revealing a complex pattern that varies significantly with the time of year and heliocentric distance, but the most influential factor is always the distribution of solar wind speed itself. This study investigates the behavior of a planar shock wave with a high adiabatic index, specifically looking at how it affects the formation of a singularity at the origin. We consider the case where the adiabatic index exceeds a critical threshold, causing the shock wave to develop a singular ITZESki structure - a shape with an infinite curvature at the origin. Our primary goal is to analyze this singular scenario and demonstrate that it can be represented through the use of a specific transformation, namely the Lewis transformation, which extends the initial data beyond the origin. Furthermore, we successfully apply this transformation to obtain the exact solution for this particular type of shock wave, effectively expanding the domain of existing solutions. We also compare it with the existing singular ITZESki structure caused by a point source, revealing distinct features. Additionally, we examine the transition to the Taylor shock wave by varying the strength of the shock, and observe that the change occurs abruptly, and is influenced by the adiabatic index. Our research also reveals the existence of a critical adiabatic index, above which the shock wave cannot maintain its integrity and will instead break into two separate shocks, one of which is a rarefaction wave and the other a shock wave with the above-mentioned singular structure. We have been able to determine the lower and upper bounds of this critical index, which interestingly enough, are the same, and we have explored how it changes with time. Our study provides the first detailed analysis of this singular structure, which we have found to be stable, and with our new solution, we believe it is worthy of inclusion in the established self-similar solutions for shock waves. This study develops a detailed analysis of B meson decays into two vector mesons, focusing on the use of the upgraded ATLAS detector to explore rare, rare transition processes. Initially, a general description of B meson decay patterns is provided, considering both $B\rightarrow V_1 V_2$ and $B\rightarrow V_1 V_1 \gamma$ decays, where $V_1$ and $V_2$ represent vector mesons. Given the significance of these processes in understanding the properties of the W boson and the presence of New Physics, researchers outline the potential of the ATLAS experiment to investigate these processes with higher precision, using data from the LHC operating at 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 3 ab$^{-1}$. This would enable researchers to achieve optimal sensitivity in measuring low-probability transitions, such as $b\rightarrow s\gamma$ and $d\rightarrow u$ gauge interactions, with predicted efficiencies of 100 to 1000 times greater than those of existing experiments, the Large Hadron Electron Collider and the upgraded top quark pair production experiments. The proposed search utilizes optimized variables to enhance sensitivity, including the use of new variables in $J/\psi \rho^0$ and $K^* K^* \gamma$ final states. We develop a distributed optimization algorithm for a cooperative system consisting of multiple agents, some of which may intentionally disrupt communication. To compensate for the negative impacts of malicious agents, we introduce a concept called effective connectivity, which represents the communication connectivity between cooperative agents despite interference from malice. Building on this idea, we devise a distributed algorithm utilizing two networks: one for optimal parameter estimation and the other for smooth gradient approximation. As a result, we derive an optimal solution to the distributional optimization problem. To validate our method, we provide two connectivity metrics and analyze their relationship with effective connectivity. Furthermore, we establish bounds on the convergence rate of the distributed algorithm. Simulations conducted on two examples confirm the effectiveness of our approach. Ultimately, our research enables efficient cooperation among diverse agents in complex systems by reinforcing effective connectivity. This is demonstrated through the specific application of a cooperative swarm of drones. We have discovered two likely globular cluster candidates in scan data from the North American Telescope at the Puerto Escondido Astronomical Station in Mexico. The clusters, named PEAS 9 and PEAS 10, are located at right ascensions of 13h 30m 36s and 13h 31m 42s, with declinations of -12° 16' 12" and -12° 17' 24" respectively. The discovery observations for PEAS 9 and PEAS 10 cover 84 and 90 minutes of arc on the sky and allow the estimation of stellar densities at 4.5 to 5.0 kpc from the Sun. Based on their position, distance, and the absence of variable star populations, it's believed that both clusters have ages ranging from 10 to 13 billion years and possess central black hole masses of 10 to the power of 2 dot 5 and 10 to the power of 3 dot 5 dot solar masses. The clusters' properties also suggest they may be associated with the Sagittarius tidal stream, specifically with the Sagittarius III, IV, and V globular clusters. The possible connection to the Sagittarius stream is further supported by the clusters' location in relation to the stream's center and major arms. The current data consists of 7 and 10 stellar candidates each for PEAS 9 and PEAS 10, and more in depth analysis is needed to confirm the clusters' structures and exact properties. The possible connection to the Sagittarius stream adds another aspect to these clusters' intriguing stories that require further investigation. In order to enhance the efficiency of businesses, they are increasingly relying on prediction models to automate and streamline processes like customer segmentation, inventory management, and credit risk assessment. However, the limitations of these models become apparent during deployment, given the significant gap between their performance on training data and real-world applications. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in processes with multiple stages, where earlier stages influence later ones, as shown by studies on prediction flows. These studies reveal substantial differences in model performance across stages, which can be characterized as performance patterns. In the current study, we gather existing knowledge on prediction flows and expand on the concept of performance patterns by examining the inconsistencies in model performance mentioned in research papers. Furthermore, we highlight potential pitfalls in model performance and explore strategies for enhancing the performance of models in stages with inconsistent data, including techniques as diverse as data preparation, machine learning methods, and theoretical models. We then establish relationships between these spaces and the existing Gelfand-Shilov spaces $M_{\sigma}(\Omega)$ and $S_{\sigma}(\Omega)$, demonstrating that the former spaces are consistently more robust than the latter in regards to functional mappings. Next, we prove that when equipped with the Grothendieck-Lizorkin space norm, one of the new spaces, $M_{\sigma}(\Omega_h)$, serve as an intermediate space between the original Gelfand-Shilov spaces and the Roumand-Duarte spaces, thereby facilitating the extension of the classical Paley-Wiener theorem to the case of hyperbolic Hessians. Additionally, we also derive accurate estimates for functions within the new spaces and the associated heat kernels, which in turn lead to refined convergence rates for the approximation of functions by means of the Bergman series. The RPA method has been successfully applied to investigate the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O, specifically the RPA pole calculations which correspond to the main component of the E1 strength in this nucleus. By utilizing a harmonic oscillator basis with a 0d shell occupation, previous research demonstrated that there are three distinct RPA spurious bands of 1-, 3-, and 5- phonon types that collectively contribute to the width of the E1 strength distribution. However, a harmonic oscillator basis does not accurately reflect the actual distribution of the E1 strength in $^{16}$O, which is better modeled using a Woods-Saxon basis. Our study indicates that the E1 strength in this nucleus is primarily characterized by two RPA phonon combinations: the direct transition from the 1p$_{3/2}$ to 0d$_{5/2}$ and the 1p$_{1/2}$ to 0d$_{3/2}$ orbits, and the phonon coupling involving the 1-, 3-, and 5- phonon spurious RPA bands. Our results also reveal the significant contributions of the 1p shell to the E1 strength, particularly in the lower energy range of the giant resonance, and that the current generation of e+ e- colliders will be capable of reaching the energies required to study the 1p shell electrons in the context of electric dipole photon scattering off the $^{16}$O nucleus. Nonetheless, the 1p shell's smaller contribution to the total E1 strength means that the 1p$_{1/2}$ and 1p$_{3/2}$ shells' influences are rather distinct, with the 1p$_{3/2}$ shell's contribution more evenly distributed between the RPA phonon combinations, whereas the 1p$_{1/2}$ shell's contribution is primarily associated with the 3-phonon RPA band. Therefore, an in-depth analysis of the RPA method within a harmonic oscillator basis, as well as a comparison with a more accurate Woods-Saxon basis, is necessary to thoroughly understand the E1 strength distribution in $^{16}$O. Our study paves the way for investigating the RPA method's applications in other nuclei using the harmonic oscillator basis. This study explores the application of the Koopman operator framework to analyze nonlinear dynamical systems with localized observations. Due to the presence of nonlinear relationships, it's challenging to make predictions about a system's behavior using traditional linear methods. To overcome this limitation, the Koopman operator provides a linear framework for analyzing nonlinear dynamics through localized observations. However, most existing studies in the field have been limited to using global observables, which can lead to incomplete system state reconstructions, particularly when observing nonlinear systems locally. To address this challenge, we introduce a new approach using a linear stochastic model to represent the Koopman operator, which enables the use of non-equilibrium localized observables. This innovation allows us to reconstruct the system's state from local observations in areas distant from the observation points. We apply and evaluate this method on a nonlinear diffusion model and find it to be an effective tool for state reconstruction from local observations. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach can be coupled with nonlinear control methods to achieve state feedback control. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of adding noise to the model and find that it must be considered carefully to ensure accurate system state reconstruction. Overall, this research highlights the potential of the Koopman operator framework in conjunction with linear stochastic models to seamlessly integrate with linear control techniques, enabling the state feedback control of nonlinear diffusion systems even when only local observations are available. We envision that this study will serve as a initial step towards developing a controller for nonlinear diffusion junctions with delayed state feedback. This research is an invitation to the community to explore and refine the findings presented. Neural text generation performance can be enhanced by improving sentence representations. A novel approach called SparseGAN achieves this representation improvement by applying regularization to intermediate neural network layers. Unlike common practice, SparseGAN generates dense sentence encodings, which are reduced to sparse, significant features through layer-wise $l_1$ regularization. This technique facilitates the generation of dense representations that capture essential, exception-free language patterns, thereby reducing representation dimensions. We demonstrate the benefits of SparseGAN in multiple settings, including trained models and neural sequence generation models, where it enhances the accuracy of next-word predictions and reduces the entropy of representations. The resulting models exhibit a significant decrease in representation dimensions with minimal computational overhead, allowing for smaller model architectures. We validate SparseGAN across six text generation tasks and show that it yields representative encodings that effectively capture linguistic structure, leading to improved generation performance. Animal population studies often struggle with obtaining accurate and up-to-date density estimates. A major issue with traditional methods is having sufficient population data, requiring instead the incorporation of capture-history information. We present a user-friendly R function,'sepcar', that implements a standardized approach to fitting advanced capture-recapture models with relaxation times for various movement patterns. This function generates accurate density estimates from a growing number of models that account for animal movements, particularly useful for modeling large, nomadic populations. Such models are particularly valuable for making informed management decisions in management units with low data availability. A case study involving Yellowstone's bison population demonstrates the application of these methods in practice. Additionally, the function includes corrections for both overestimation and underestimation of capture-recapture model density estimates.'sepcar' integrates density estimate models with capture-recapture analysis via the 'JAGS' library, allowing for Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation and providing capture-history probability estimates for future studies. This approach is highly versatile and can be used in conjunction with various capture strategies and for analyzing both single and multi-species population data sets. We developed a method to transform this subnetwork into an equivalent single-layer network, which we call its "shadow network." We observed that the dynamics of the outer layer's interactions influence the shadow network's properties, such as its degree distribution and weight, which in turn affect the stability of the inner layer's states. Furthermore, we found that the shadow network can be accurate even when the original inner layer consists of multiple non-overlapping components, even in dynamic conditions. Our approach has practical applications in assessing the stability of complex multilayer systems, such as those found in the human brain, financial networks, and power grids. We establish a comprehensive framework for differential modules that incorporates an expanded concept of operator equivalence. Within this expanded framework, we demonstrate the significance of operator pairs consisting of the differential operator and a scalar multiplication operator in relation to a coherent module over a differential algebra. Furthermore, we investigate the concept of an operator that is potentially parametrized by another operator within the context of differential modules. Building on the framework established by Ritt and von Zeipel, we develop the notion of an operator that is potentially parametrized by another operator as follows: given an operator pair consisting of the differential operator and a scalar multiplication operator in relation to a coherent module over a differential algebra, we define the set of operator pairs as the set of modules with defined operators, denoted by D$\mathcal{A}$. Additionally, we examine the condition under which an operator is considered to be parametrized by another operator, i.e., the operators D and $\delta$ are equivalent under the action of the module's automorphisms, i.e., (f)_{\mathfrak{c}}D = fdf^{-1} $\circ$ f_{\mathfrak{c}}$\delta$f_{\mathfrak{c}}^{-1} for some module automorphism f belonging to the group F_{\mathfrak{c}}. Moreover, we investigate the relationship between this operator equivalence and the differential module's integral manifolds. By extending the concept of an operator that is potentially parametrized by another operator to a global scale, i.e., all modules with defined operators D$\mathcal{A}$ are operator-equivalent, we demonstrate that this condition is necessary and sufficient for integrating the system's differential equations along integral curves. Finally, we provide an example illustrating the application of this concept to a nonlinear system of differential equations. Moreover, we show that the system's integral manifolds can be determined from the distribution defined by the operator-equivalent differential module. By leveraging the underlying structure of the software, it identifies potential sources of errors and suggests fixes. In contrast, the size of the software does not significantly impact its performance. This algorithm is distinctive due to its minimal communication requirements, as it allows each node to exchange information with only two neighbors. The proposed method's precision can also be enhanced through additional intra-network communications, revealing a promising pathway for further optimization. The algorithm's precision and communication complexity make it a promising solution for numerous large-scale network applications. Researchers utilized high-resolution electrocortical recordings from the visual and motor areas of patients with traumatic brain injuries to develop decoding models for predicting walking capabilities. By comparing the accuracy of high-resolution electrocortical recordings from the cerebral cortex at different depths, a significant precision advantage was discovered in recordings from the superficial layers of the motor area. A proposed decoding framework that combines shallow network architecture and training data curation demonstrated a 13% boost in decoding precision within the motor area and a 7% boost in the visual area through data selection. When evaluating the proposed method on new data, a 24% improvement in decoding precision was found in the motor area and a 13% improvement in the visual area. Furthermore, the proposed framework showed a 13% better precision than conventional EEG methods in decoding cortical signals from cortical recordings. Additionally, accurate walking function predictions were made using a novel approach that combines recurrent neural networks and multivariate generalized additive models, resulting in a 16% better precision than traditional regression analysis. Lastly, a positive correlation was discovered between the accuracy of walking function predictions and the complexity of the model, explaining the need for careful network architecture and model selection to achieve the best decoding results. Furthermore, the validity of the proposed framework was validated through a re-decoding exercise involving the same data, demonstrating a 33% better precision than chance in both areas. We investigate the long-term behavior of right-angled Artin groups that act on trees via graph covering spaces. Our analysis focuses on actions resulting from a specific generating process, which we call the "branching expansion" scenario. Within this context, we identify a significant subgraph in the group's definition, termed a "separating subgraph," which enables us to establish a connection between this subgraph and a specific branch of the group's action on the tree. This connection allows us to demonstrate that there exists a first branch that eventually becomes "stable" as time progresses. We further establish that the existing separating subgraph within this stable branch shares characteristics similar to those of the original subgraph, which we term "approximate self-similarity." Ultimately, our findings converge to results previously established by Horbeck and Schleper in their investigation of free groups. The approach we employ is inspired by their "cutting sequence" technique, yet our execution is distinct due to the inherent differences between free groups and right-angled Artin groups. Additionally, our research paves the way for an examination of the dynamic behavior of groups associated with expanding systems exhibiting multiple expanding directions. We also introduce a broader class of groups linked to these systems, which we call "higher branch groups," and explore their theoretical properties. Many real-world systems, including cultural networks and neural connections, evolve over time, meaning their representations must be both dynamic and complex. Current graph representation learning models typically focus on static graphs and have several limitations when applied to temporal graphs, leading to low performance. To overcome these limitations, we develop a new framework called DECENNT, a dynamic graph neural network, to accurately predict node degrees in temporal graphs by incorporating both temporal patterns and complex graph structures. DECENNT consists of a Degree Predictor and a Dynamic updater, enhancing both model flexibility and interpretability. Through extensive experiments on 5 datasets, DECENNT demonstrates significant improvements in predicting node degrees on temporal graphs compared to existing methods, surpassing the current state-of-the-art models by a wide margin. Additionally, DECENNT provides insights into the relationships between node degrees and their temporal patterns, demonstrating its potential to enhance our understanding of complex systems and their evolution. Furthermore, DECENNT's performance is evaluated in a node degree recommendation task and a graph reconstruction task, showing that it excels in both cases. To facilitate further research, DECENNT is implemented using PyTorch and openly available on GitHub. With its superior performance and intuitive dynamics, DECENNT presents a valuable framework for representing and predicting the evolution of complex graph systems. To ensure reproducibility, the code and datasets used in this study are accessible via the following links: https://github.com/zhongyu-wei/DECENNT and https://github.com/zhongyu-wei/Datasets_DECENNT. Moreover, DECENNT has been successfully applied to a new dataset described in a companion paper titled Understanding Node Degree Evolution in Temporal Graphs Using DECENNT. Both the code and datasets are developed and made publicly accessible as part of this research project. We are happy to share the DECENNT model and related resources with the scientific community. Analyzing the movements of various entities within images is a challenge that arises in multiple applications such as biology, security, and sports analysis.  In many cases, distinguishing biological movements from non-biological movements is crucial.  This task is particularly difficult due to the complex patterns of movement that can be present in images and the uncertainty associated with their boundaries.  To address this challenge, researchers have developed a method that utilizes convolutional neural networks to produce probability maps which are then converted into score images that reflect the likelihood of representing biological movement.  To account for the uncertainty associated with the movements' boundaries, a convolutional Gaussian process is employed, all within a convolutional neural network framework.  This method has been put into practice on a dataset consisting of images related to pedestrian activity.  To effectively evaluate the performance of this method, a metric is employed that considers the accuracy of its predictions in areas where the probability of biological movement is high.  As a result, this research provides a solution to a wide range of movement analysis challenges while also demonstrating how the integration of convolutional neural networks and Gaussian processes can be accomplished efficiently.  This combined technique involves sharing the network's weights across multiple evaluations, significantly reducing the computation required.  This effort also involves developing a novel Gaussian process convolutional neural network training algorithm that enables the integration of expert knowledge into the Gaussian process weight prior.  This prior represents the probability distribution of the network's weights and allows the model to be taught with sparse, expert-annotated data. We introduce the Nested Neumann algorithm, an efficient method for computing the inception complexity of a scalar function along curves on manifold-valued datasets. We demonstrate the algorithm's convergence within a specific number of iterations that is directly proportional to the inception depth of the function. Specifically, we show that the algorithm requires O(1/(η^2)) iterations to achieve a specific inception depth η for a particular class of Riemannian functions. We also investigate the relationship between the inception complexity and the algorithm's convergence, finding it is directly proportional to the square of the inception depth. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence and experimental results on real and synthetic datasets, highlighting the benefits of inception complexity in machine learning. Our research proposes the Nested Neumann algorithm and provides theoretical and practical evidence for the importance of inception complexity in a broader context of optimization on manifold-valued datasets. In contextual linear bandits, it is crucial to explore the environment efficiently while mastering the underlying dynamics, as the optimal policy is heavily influenced by the context distribution. We introduce a new phase-based approach that achieves a time-dependent confidence interval, allowing us to establish a lower bound on the bit count that needs to be learned about the context distribution over time. This result demonstrates that the bit count also follows a polynomial growth curve, thereby being included in the class of time-dependent functions that can be learned effectively using our phase-based method. Our algorithm utilizes a versatile phase-based framework that is adaptable to various context distributions and learning objectives, which it extends to regulate contextual linear bandits. Our main result reveals that this algorithm acquires an optimal understanding of the context distribution rapidly, as well as obtains the optimal policy within a polynomial number of interactions and bit counts that grow in a specific, non-autonomous linear manner. These findings collectively complement our theoretical insights with a practical solution, as they show that the context distribution's knowledge can be mastered with an extremely efficient bit count, as supported by our non-autonomous polynomial learning theory. Our rigorous execution of the phase-based framework ensures that the resulting algorithm achieves the same optimal regret and bit count bounds that are derived through our non-autonomous polynomial learning theory with a general context distribution. As a separate contribution, we also establish a non-autonomous polynomial learning theory that extends the conventional polynomial learning setting with a fixed parameter that marks the end of the learning phase, as it allows for the context distribution's knowledge to be captured with a growing, rather than a fixed, number of bits. This non-autonomous extension incorporates a novel time-dependent parameter that influences the bit count in a polynomial manner, as it provides a general context in which the bit count learning can be described through the change of a parameter that marks the end of the learning phase. Our non-autonomous learning setting also includes a benchmark algorithm that is known to follow the desired bit count trajectory, as it enables the incorporation of algorithms that already satisfy the desired bit count requirements, as well as providing a natural way to extend the existing polynomial learning theory to a non-autonomous setting. Our non-autonomous learning setting is versatile and context-independent, as it can be applied to various context distributions, as well as learning objectives that are defined by the bit count trajectories. For policy learning using efficient value function estimates, selecting the optimal sample size for testing can be critical. This study examines how test sample size influences the policy learning outcome when combining model-based and model-free data. Our findings show that with small test samples, our proposed efficient value function estimate performs significantly better than alternative methods. However, as the test sample size increases, the difference in performance diminishes. Our efficient value function estimate exhibits stable policy learning performance across various sample sizes, including large ones. In contrast, alternative approaches experience declining performance with increasing sample sizes. In scenarios with medium to large test sample sizes, our efficient value function estimate performs similarly to or even worse than other methods. Nonetheless, our estimate demonstrates consistent performance advantages, especially in situations with limited data. This advantage is most pronounced in expensive policy learning settings, such as those requiring numerous interactions with a costly black-box policy. Our research proposes several possible explanations for these findings, including the risk of overfitting and differences in robustness to sample size. To facilitate policy learning with varying sample sizes, we provide a robust policy learning algorithm that accounts for different value function estimate methods. This algorithm's performance can be evaluated using our efficient value function estimate and alternative methods. Our work contributes to policy learning with efficient value function estimates, offering a way to combine different value function estimates and providing a robust policy learning algorithm that accommodates diverse value function estimate approaches. In addition to its general applicability, our research provides useful insights and algorithms for challenging policy learning settings, such as those requiring numerous interactions with a costly black-box policy. In these scenarios, our algorithm using the efficient value function estimate results in policy learning outcomes that are close to optimal. In contrast, alternative methods often yield significantly poorer outcomes. Our code is available on a public repository.

In large wireless communication networks, implementing power control algorithms can effectively manage interference. However, calculating the optimal power control settings for multiple overlapping connections can be computationally costly. To address this challenge, a simple and efficient binary power control algorithm has been developed, which allows for dynamic management of interference by switching between high and low power settings. According to the findings, after an initial adjustment period, the performance of binary power control converges to the optimal power control performance, with a rate of convergence directly influenced by the duration of switch intervals. To be more precise, the performance difference between the two settings can be achieved in a number of switch intervals that is proportional to the square of the ratio of high to low power settings. As a result, it is recommended to use the algorithm with tight power ratio controls, as it can lead to significant computational savings while maintaining optimal performance in large scale networks. Experimental data from a real-world application is also presented. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the algorithm's performance complements existing optimal power control strategies, which often serve as initial power settings for the binary algorithm. Consequently, a combined strategy that alternates between binary power control and optimal power control can be highly effective, as shown in the results presented. The goal was to maximize the total amount of video streamed within a fixed time frame of ten minutes. Unfortunately, the physical interactions between a robot and a deformable surface can cause a robot's legs to lose synchronization, making it difficult to track intended trajectories. In response to this challenge, researchers are leveraging feedback control techniques to ensure that robotic legs maintain the necessary synchronization to hop along desired trajectories. While previous studies have focused on feeding back to variables like foot velocity and foot height, a newly developed method directs feedback to a more fundamental variable: the dimensionalless phase of each robotic leg. In a model representing a single robotic leg interacting with a deformable surface, a state-space representation is created and a robust feedback control system is designed to track specific trajectories. In a demonstration involving a four-legged robotic hopper, feedback control to the dimensionalless phase of each leg enhances the accuracy of trajectory tracking, significantly outperforming a baseline controller. A novel method for computing meson charge radii in perturbation theory has been developed, where the use of a non-zero charge parameter $\alpha$ in the quark mass parameter is crucial. This approach involves the calculation of two cross terms that arise from the product of the electric charge and the light quark mass in the relativistic relativistic energy expression for mesons. A key step in this method involves employing the relation between the charge radius and the anomalous dimension of the mass operator, and has been applied to $J^P = 1^-$ meson states ($q\bar{q}$ and $s\bar{s}$) using the relativized perturbation theory. Numerical calculations of charge radii for these mesons have been performed, and the results show that the variation of the charge radius with the quark mass is proportional to the average of the quark and antiquark masses. Additionally, predictions for the charge radii of heavier meson states, including $D$ and $B$ mesons, have been obtained from the application of the relativized perturbation theory. A key finding of this study is the small difference in charge radii between mesons composed of different quark flavors, which can be attributed to the small effect of flavor dependence due to the small variation in average quark masses. A calculated value of $1.94 \pm 0.33$ fm has been derived for the charm meson $D$ charge radius, which is found to be only slightly larger than that of the up quark, and is expected to be relevant in the study of meson radii in heavy ion collisions. A predicted value of $1.63 \pm 0.29$ fm has also been obtained for the beauty meson $B$ charge radius, which is similar in size to that of the strange quark. A proposed experiment to measure the charm meson $D$ charge radius using the PANDA experiment at the Future Circular Collider is also suggested. A calculation of meson charge radii using the relativistic mean-field theory in the Walecka model has been compared with the perturbation theory results. The analysis of complex information networks, particularly those comprising textual data, has given rise to multiple probabilistic models, including the Hierarchical Document Topic Model. This model has shown a superior performance record in comparison to conventional statistical methods for tasks such as classification, recommendation, and the analysis of information networks themselves. However, implementing models of this nature is computationally intensive due to the need for repeated evaluation of the model's likelihood. To address this challenge, a Stochastic Hierarchical Document Topic Model is proposed, which is a compact variation of the HDTM, featuring a fixed structure and randomly selected topic assignments. This model can be trained on large data sets with extensive networks in a relatively efficient manner, with results showing it maintains a high degree of similarity to the original HDTM across a range of evaluation metrics. As evidence of the model's versatility, the proposed method is demonstrated to be a viable approximation technique for models with hierarchical structures, in addition to providing a straightforward implementation of the HDTM. The technical feasibility of this model is supported by a comprehensive experimental study, covering both static and dynamic information networks, with results revealed in the subsequent sections. Quantum annealing's effectiveness relies on its ability to navigate the complex landscape of energy minima, but understanding the annealing process's dynamics remains challenging. The annealing gap, the difference between the quantum Ramsey ramp and the classical system's localization width, is a crucial factor that can be optimized for, but its behavior throughout the process is not well characterized. We investigate the annealing gap's evolution under various conditions and its relationship with the quantum Ramsey ramp's structure, finding that it initially increases before entering a chaotic phase, but we also find that its dynamics can be controlled by adjusting the annealing schedule, leading to the possibility of optimized protocols. Our study focuses on a spin-interaction system and a hybrid quantum-classical simulator, but we believe our findings are broadly applicable to other systems and devices. We propose that the annealing gap's dynamics should be a key consideration in quantum annealing protocols, potentially leading to more efficient solutions. Our research demonstrates the importance of considering the annealing gap's behavior in efficient solution finding through quantum annealing. Additionally, we provide a simple, scalable method to incorporate the annealing gap into quantum annealing's energy function, which we test on a genetic algorithm as well, and observe improved success rates and shorter execution times. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the annealing gap and quantum tunneling, which may be a promising area for future research. A comprehensive theoretical investigation of the electronic structure and subsequent magnetic and superconducting properties in 4e-band nickelates is presented. These nickelates have the general formula (LAO)_2(RNiO_3.5), where LAO stands for strontium and oxygen, and L = lithium, sodium. The band structure, effective magnetic moments, and possible superconducting pairing mechanisms are examined in (Li,Na)NiO_3.5. The results show that these materials are antiferromagnetic and d-wave superconducting, with the superconducting phase being separated from the antiferromagnetic phase by an orbital excitonic mechanism. The effective magnetic moments are consistent with experimental neutron scattering findings. The presence of extra electrons in the 4e-band Nickelates makes them intriguing objects for study, with complex band structures influencing their physical properties. The results of this study demonstrate how the band structure drives the antiferromagnetic and superconducting phases in these materials, and could potentially guide experimental research in this field. The absence of any on-site spin-orbit interaction in these materials means that orbital excitons can form without a corresponding reduction in effective magnetic moments. The antiferromagnetic phase can be achieved without any additional parameters when the parent lattice is considered alone, making the theoretical model presented here straightforward to apply, while the inclusion of extra electrons in the 4e-band Nickelates differentiates them from other rare-earth elements based on transition metals. The theoretical investigation of these materials also considers a slightly distorted parent lattice, which is consistent with experimental findings, and includes the effects of next-nearest-neighbor hoppings on the band structure, to ensure an accurate match with experimental data. The consequences of these interactions on the physical properties of these materials are significant, with the distortion of the parent lattice influencing the orientation of effective magnetic moments, and with all components of the Hamiltonian being included in the theoretical model to ensure a comprehensive understanding of these materials. The specific materials examined in this study are lithium and sodium nickelates, which are considered ideal objects for study due to their simple crystal structure, and with the results of this study potentially guiding the optimization of these materials for improved performance. Theoretical models of quantum chromodynamics' deconfinement phase transition and quark stars were examined.  Despite the discrepancy from observed neutron star masses, a meson-pion phase transition model yielded small quark star masses.  In contrast, a polytroptic mass-radius relation resulted from the Yang-Mills phase transition model, which showed quark star radii within the observable range, however with masses below the observed limit.  We derive a simplified polytroptic model from the Yang-Mills phase transition equations of state, obtaining an explicit formula for the mass-radius relation.  This formula's characteristics were confirmed through numerical analysis, showing that the star's radius decreases with mass, in opposition to the conventional relation.  The presence of a deconfinement phase transition may influence the properties of quark stars, however more realistic equations of state are necessary for better match with observed data.  A crucial aspect is the need for a recipe to switch from the quark star to neutron star models when masses approach the phase transition point.  Two possible transition equations were tested, demonstrating their impact on the quark star model, particularly on its mass and radius.  In addition to the mass-radius relation, the gravitational oscillation frequency and the star's compressibility also demonstrated sensitive dependence on the equation of state.  In conclusion, the quark star phase transition model presents several attractive features, however more precise measurements are necessary to confirm its validity, and even then, more realistic equations of state will be necessary, involving a transition recipe that is still to be determined. One of the key advantages of using quantum systems as instruments is their enhanced sensitivity to measuring subtle parameters such as damping. The compass state, with its precise phase control and balanced superposition, exhibits notable variations in its number distribution when subject to different damping rates. To investigate the metrological utility of this state, we examine how its number variance affects the precision with which it can determine a classical system's damping constant in a 3-dimensionally confined setting. The findings indicate that the compass state's ability to accurately measure a specific damping factor depends greatly on the magnitude of that factor, with a maximum achievable precision of 0.0323, surpassing the standard quantum limit of 0.0713. The optimal damping-dependent condition is characterized and the required duration of measurement identified as 12.59 times the system's decay time. Moreover, a comparison with another balanced state reveals that the compass state's performance is indeed superior, largely due to its unique number variance characteristics. The investigation also considers the effects of number non-localization and finds that the optimal condition applies specifically to determining the damping constant from the population inversion of excited and ground states. The research on the compass state is also found to provide valuable insights into the general use of balanced quantum states in metrology. The findings demonstrate that balanced states with precise phase control can efficiently measure the amplitude of classical noise, with the compass state itself offering the highest precision of 0.0521 from a variety of balanced states examined. The optimal condition turns out to be specifically the 1-e-1 ratio characteristic commonly found in the compass state, indicating that this particular balance is the most suitable for this specific application. Knowledge questioning is a challenging task that requires a system to pose effective questions to incorporate relevant knowledge for task performance, with the goal of improving overall accuracy. To streamline this process, our approach leverages a semantic-driven framework that incorporates knowledge by asking targeted questions, with the purpose of enhancing the system's understanding of input data before making a final decision. Within this framework, we develop a multiple-choice knowledge questioning model that utilizes relevance-based scoring to evaluate potential answers to its questions. By incorporating this model into the semantic-driven framework, we enhance the system's ability to ask more precise questions that are directly related to the task at hand, with the result being a system that asks fewer questions while achieving the same level of accuracy. Furthermore, our approach enhances the system's ability to identify alternative knowledge that contradicts its current understanding, with the consequence being a significant decrease in the number of questions it needs to ask to reach a correct solution. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on multiple datasets across three different applications, with the outcome showing a substantial improvement in accuracy achieved by the system with the current approach in comparison to a random knowledge questioning model, with the accuracy increase ranging from 1.43% to 13.83%. Additionally, our approach was found to yield comparable performance to a system that asks unlimited questions, with the further benefit of being more scalable. In terms of model size, we observed a significant reduction in the required parameters for our multiple-choice knowledge questioning model, with the result being a more efficient system that is more adaptable to various tasks and datasets, with the resulting model being up to 97% smaller in parameter size. In addition to its practical implications, our approach has theoretical significance in relation to the knowledge questioning task, with the consequence being a more challenging problem that requires a more sophisticated model. To demonstrate this, we created a theoretical example that shows the need for a model utilizing relevance-based scoring in order to provide a correct solution. Moreover, our approach has a positive impact on the system's ability to handle paradoxical knowledge, with the effect being a significant decrease in the system's guess rate when confronting alternative knowledge, with the rate decrease ranging from 23.85% to 93.75% in comparison to a random knowledge questioning model. With the aim of verifying the generalizability of our approach, we conducted additional experiments using the same datasets and settings but with the difference being the removal of paradoxical knowledge, with the outcome showing no decline in accuracy achieved by the system. For prison inmates, mental health treatments are typically part of a broader rehabilitation plan aimed at reducing future crimes.  However, different treatments may have varying levels of success in achieving this broad goal.  To better understand the underlying dynamics, we treat prison recidivism as a result of multiple factors, including factors such as a prisoner's characteristics, social interactions, and participation in activities. A common challenge faced in semi-supervised medical image segmentation arises from labeled data being too limited to effectively train convolutional neural networks, leading to poor generalization performance.  Our proposed method, SSNet, strives to enhance regularization through a new interpolation-based mixing strategy for patch-level labels, ensuring consistency across different views of an image. Evaluations conducted on MRI brain lesion segmentation datasets (MISTY and PBCS) demonstrate improved performance compared to leading semi-supervised techniques.  The code and models developed are available for public use on GitHub.  Future work plans are outlined with a particular focus on extending our approach to include more complex networks and real-world clinical applications. To gain a deeper understanding of material properties and behaviors, researchers have been using graph neural networks to analyze and model atomic structures within materials. Although successful in predicting various physical properties and identifying phases from simulations, most existing approaches process raw distance matrices without considering the inherent chemical information present in bond connections. This limitation makes the learned representations prone to noise, potentially leading to models that are either overly complex or fail to generalize. In contrast, our study proposes a novel strategy for incorporating chemical information into distance-based neural networks by using a graph attention mechanism, which focuses on critical bond connections, thereby reducing unnecessary information. By leveraging this approach in our message passing neural network, we gain a more precise representation of local atomic configurations. We demonstrate the benefits of our method by accurately predicting the energy of atoms in a cluster, identifying phases from supercell configurations, and quantifying local configurations from defects in solid solutions. Our approach has the potential to enhance existing models by incorporating more precise representations of atomic configurations. Our code is available at https://github.com/QianQian-Li/GANN_for_materials.

The main purpose of this paper is to demonstrate how the weak convergence of sequential estimates can be applied to achieve functional estimates of parameters. We achieve this by utilizing the functional delta-method, a version of the delta-method suited for functions that are not differentiable. The functional delta-method can be seen as a natural extension of the original delta-method, and it enables us to estimate functions of parameters by considering the behavior of the functional application to sequential estimates of the parameter itself. We then apply the functional delta-method to several examples involving negative binomial point process models and Poisson random field models. These examples illustrate the practical utility of the functional delta-method in its current form. Additionally, we provide a version of the functional delta-method that is tailored to the strong metric, which we refer to as the strong delta-method. This can be utilized to establish the weak convergence of functionals of sequential estimates when the initial distribution is known. We then extend the strong delta-method to a scenario involving an unknown initial distribution. We refer to this as the empirical delta-method. We apply the empirical delta-method to a count process model involving negative binomial distributions. Furthermore, we offer two versions of the empirical delta-method: one that utilizes the sample mean as an estimate of the initial mean, and another that utilizes a greater empirical efficiency. We also provide a version of the empirical delta-method that can handle functionals of multiple parameters. We then combine the empirical delta-method with the functional delta-method to estimate a function of multiple parameters from count process observations. We conclude by highlighting the practical applications and theoretical implications of our proposed methods. We also address the challenge of obtaining consistent empirical estimates of the functional delta-method parameter, which we refer to as the Euler score. We propose two solutions to this issue: one involves utilizing a random cut-off time to obtain a consistent estimator of the Euler score, and the other involves combining the empirical delta-method with the functional delta-method. We then explore the properties of these proposed methods through simulated simulations and real-data examples. We also provide the code for these experiments in the supplementary materials available online. We hope that our research will contribute to the development of statistical inference methods for complex models and systems. We also believe that our proposed methods have the potential to be applied in various research fields. We also plan to explore the relationship between the weak convergence of sequential estimates and the strong convergence of the empirical process. We also aim to investigate the properties of the Euler score in more detail. We also plan to apply the functional delta-method to a model involving Gaussian process distributions.

Deep learning knowledge tracing evaluation methods are diverse and often require a vast amount of data for tuning, which can be challenging to obtain in many real-world applications, especially when data is limited. A team from the Knowledge Engineering Research Lab at the University of Houston conducted an extensive review of 19 diverse deep learning knowledge tracing models and evaluation methods. They analyzed the models' underlying theories, learning mechanisms, and performance assessment methods, which they presented in a structured framework. Furthermore, they developed a synthetic dataset to compare the performance of different models and evaluation methods through rigorous experiments. Interestingly, their results showed that models and evaluation methods often produce similar performance when tested on both real and synthetic data. This finding suggests that deep learning knowledge tracing models and evaluation methods are, in part, based on random patterns in existing datasets rather than accurately capturing underlying learning dynamics. Consequently, the authors propose a simple knowledge tracing dataset that captures common learning patterns to facilitate fair evaluation of models and evaluation methods. This dataset along with their comprehensive framework and experimental results will facilitate further research on deep learning knowledge tracing. Given a smooth function f belonging to the domain of the second-order elliptic differential operator Δ, we investigate conditions under which the operator Δ - s is surjective within the space of functions with a certain decay rate, denoted by Hs(ℝn). Our primary goal is to establish that for a certain class of functions f, the operator Δ - s is surjective within Hs(ℝn) if it is invariant with respect to a specific parabolic group G∞(ℝn). Furthermore, we provide an alternative criterion linking the surjectivity of Δ - s to the behavior of the operator Δ - s on the space of functions with a certain smoothness, denoted by Hs+1/2(ℝn). Moreover, we demonstrate the significance of these results in the context of the Schrödinger operator H = -Δ + V. Finally, we also consider the relation between the surjectivity of Δ - s and the Mihlin-Hormand operator Δ -s acting on the space of functions with a certain derivative decay rate, denoted by H1,∞(ℝn). Our study builds upon the theoretical framework established by Hörmander in his 1985 work "The Spectrum of Positive Elliptic Operators". Our approach also draws inspiration from the results obtained by Hörmander as well as the more recent findings by Sjöstrand and Taylor in their 1980 paper "Lapidus (ed.): Mathematical Quantum Physics. Journees mathematiques relatives a la theorie quantique du champ" within the "Mathematical Quantum Physics" conference proceedings. Our research extends the surjectivity properties of the operator Δ - s beyond those identified by Hörmander by broadening the domain from Hs(ℝn) to Hs+1/2(ℝn) following a novel approach that prioritizes geometric considerations over the use of pseudodifferential operators. By introducing a distinct method that focuses on the composition of operators, we are able to demonstrate a new instance of surjectivity within the space of functions with a certain decay rate, building upon the specific case studied by Hörmander, which involved a constant multiplier operator. Our work ultimately aims to contribute to the understanding of the relationship between the surjectivity of the operator Δ - s and the behavior of the Schrödinger operator H = -Δ + V.
