This understanding allows us to reframe several key issues, such as the limitations of CNNs in handling non-Euclidean data and the relationship between GCNs and neural networks, in a new light. We have also discovered that by modifying the graph associated with a network, we can circumvent certain inductive biases built into its architecture, thereby enabling it to handle a broader range of inputs and output types. We have further observed that this technique can be used to extend the capabilities of both CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks. We have tested this approach on various problems and found it to be effective in predicting the physical properties of molecules, classifying text as language or mathematical expressions, and generating mathematical expressions from physical data, among other tasks. We have also explored the methodology on more complex models like Self-Supervised Neural Networks and Graph Neural Networks. Our framework and associated methods can be used as a foundation for integrating the strengths of different learning tasks and expanding the capacity of learning models to accommodate changing input types and related physical properties, all without the need for task-specific training or data. We have made our code and protocols available at https://github.com/Qianhewu/GraphConvNet. We conduct an in-depth examination of rotating, "hairy" black holes within the context of Chern-Simons gravity, focusing on its pure form. The study compares the entropy of these black holes to those predicted by the Hawking-Hubeny approach, modified to accommodate Chern-Simons theory. The analysis reveals that the proposed model accurately captures the entropy characteristics of black holes featuring Chern-Simons terms in all dimensions. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the Hawking-Hubeny formula extends its applicability to include rotating black holes in various spacetime dimensions, providing a unified framework for understanding the entropy of these black holes. The study also clarifies the relationship between the Hawing-Hubeny approach and the Wald approach to calculating black hole entropy within the Chern-Simons gravity context. The results presented can serve as a foundation for extending the analysis to include charged and rotating black holes in Chern-Simons gravity. The research findings specifically for the $O(3)$ sigma-model (also known as $3.1$ Chern-Simons gravity) demonstrate that this model is equivalent to a combined configuration of Einstein gravity and a specific kind of Chern-Simons modification to general relativity, thereby offering an explanation for the unusual behavior of black holes within this context. The study results are valid for both rotating and stationary black holes across any spacetime dimension. The validity of the results is demonstrated through a comparative analysis of the calculated entropy values and those obtained through other methods, including the Wald approach and the Hawking-Hubeny formula in its original form. The most notable feature of the study lies in its presentation of a generalized form of the Hawing-Hubeny formula, effectively expanding the limited spacetime dimensions for which the original formula was validated. The generalized formula reveals that the Hawing-Hubeny approach accurately captures the entropy characteristics of rotating black holes across all spacetime dimensions. The study also conducts an analysis of the conformal phase transition in the context of the $O(3)$ sigma-model, using the reduced Chern-Simons gravity as a background. The investigation demonstrates that the transition is driven by the same kind of potential as that observed in the standard 4-dimensional context, despite being inherently gravitational in nature. The research further explores the relationship between the asymptotic symmetry analysis and the conformal field theory dynamics. The study results demonstrate that the central extension of the conformal algebra is directly related to the entropy of the rotating black holes within this context. A fundamental challenge in elastography arises from the limited resolution of ultrasound systems, particularly in estimating axial displacements versus laterals. This critical issue is, however, often addressed under the assumption that axial and lateral displacements are equally precise. Yet, due to the linear array ultrasound system's nature, axial displacement estimation is typically more accurate than lateral estimation. In this work, a novel approach is introduced that incorporates the actual precision of both axial and lateral displacements in time-domain elastography. This approach is demonstrated using synthetic linear array data and in vitro goat liver tissue, and shows that the proposed method yields more reliable estimates than existing techniques, especially in regions far from the transducer, due to the more precise axial displacement estimation. As a result, this research contributes a promising technique for a more realistic and more widely applicable elastography algorithm. Furthermore, this work highlights the significance of considering the actual precision of both axial and lateral displacements, rather than assuming them as equal, for improving elastography through machine learning. In the experiments conducted, this approach resulted in accurately elastographically estimated stiffness values compared to conventional techniques, which often resulted in decreased estimation accuracy. This research paves the way for various extensions, including using training data from in vivo patients, actual elastography images from contrast agent, and nonlinear elastography, by providing a more precise and widely applicable baseline method. This approach can be further improved by utilizing more sophisticated machine learning frameworks, such as neural networks, and integrating elastography with other medical imaging modalities, such as MRI. This research has the added benefit of addressing the shift variance issue encountered in elastography through spatial compounding, and demonstrates the critical impact of precision consideration on elastography performance. This challenge-processing framework can be applied to other image processing tasks, such as ultrasound tissue typing, by incorporating specific constraints and precision estimates. Unlike conventional pseudocodes, logical pseudocodes, which are developed using a rule-based framework, possess a natural separation between computational content and declarative interpretation. This distinct separation offers a limited degree of safety within the underlying specification. However, this safety is not sufficient to guarantee the correctness of the system when considering sequential execution. This study presents an initial attempt to explore the concept of safety in logical pseudocodes through the analysis of their operational semantics using the B method. A key contribution of this work involves developing appropriate pre and post-conditions to ensure that logical pseudocodes meet certain properties, thereby facilitating the generation of correct construction algorithms. A sample application of this approach is demonstrated through the creation of a correct construction algorithm for a logical pseudocode representing a traffic controller. This algorithm was initially introduced by J.R. Driscoll et al. A notable limitation of the current approach involves the requirement that underlying pseudocodes be functionally complete, meaning that they are capable of performing calculations and making conditional statements. By balancing the need for precise local information and the benefits of simplified superstate knowledge, we dynamically adjust the size of these superstates as the pursuit-evasion progression unfolds. Our results show that by focusing on the most crucial aspects of the grid world, we can significantly reduce the size of the state space, resulting in a substantial decrease in action uncertainty and a corresponding improvement in our chances of evading the pursuing agent, especially in large-scale environments. When applying a single agent dynamics model to multiple tasks from the same domain, several challenges arise, including the need to account for different optimal policies and the potential for the model to learn unstable dynamics. To address this issue, we propose a meta-algorithm called the dynamics model sweep (DMS), which involves training a single agent dynamics model on a unified state and action space, and then uses the model to guide the training of multiple task-specific policies via policy sweep. We prove that under certain conditions, DMS results in a set of policies that are stable and optimal for the individual tasks. Furthermore, our experiments across three complex environments show that DMS achieves better performance compared to a single dynamics model and other comparison methods. In particular, DMS is shown to yield a 24% increase in return in the 4x4 Cart-Pole domain and a 21% increase in return in the Mountain Car domain, among other results. Our code is available on the repositories mentioned in the paper notes.

More significantly, such a statement can be made to appear both true and false within the system, which provides a logical means of achieving the paradoxical effect described by Russell's antipodal principle. This particular result involves two previously known mathematicians, K. Godel and J. B. Rosser, who independently developed the idea almost simultaneously. Despite its significance, this version of the theorem remains less well-known than the original results of Godel and Rosser, which may be attributed to the limited extent of Moore's related work when it was initially published. Called CWGAN, it generates synthetic data by taking a regularized approach and approximating the conditional Wasserstein distance using a neural network. CWGAN enhances the quality of generated samples and facilitates the incorporation of prior knowledge into the model by employing an additional regularization term. By using the conditional version, CWGAN can be applied to generate posterior samples, thereby facilitating the application of Bayesian methods in imaging scenarios. Observations of the millisecond pulsar PSR B1133+16, spanning 24 years, have yielded detailed information about the scattering materials surrounding it. A comprehensive analysis of both the positional data and the scattering widths of the pulsar's signals led to a detailed picture of the environment. The analysis uncovered 34 distinct scattering screens along the pulsar's line of sight, stretching from 1.4 to 17.4 kpc from Earth. These screens are thought to be the remnants of pulsar winds and ejected neutron stars in a surrounding star cluster. The research also revealed variations in the densities of the screens, with higher densities more likely in areas with more active scintillation. Furthermore, the small distance of the nearest screen, 1.4 kpc, suggests that such phenomena are likely common in the local galaxy, awaiting discovery. The study has contributed significant data to the understanding of pulsar environments and the galactic medium. The observed variations in the widths of the pulsar's signal, occurring every 0.45 years, are attributed to the pulsar moving through the cross-sectional area of a scattering screen, with the screen aligned perpendicular to the pulsar's orbital plane. The findings have also enabled estimates of the radii of the pulsar's scattering environment and its surrounding nebula, approximately 10 pc in diameter, and the average density of the nebula, equivalent to the density of the Helix Nebula. The research has further contributed to the understanding of the relationship between the densities of the screens and the pulsar's orbital periods, with implications for the treatment of scintillation in the search for continuous gravitational waves. The data has also been used to develop a model for the radiated power of the pulsar winds and the ejected neutron stars, with estimates suggesting a total radiated power of 5.6 x 10^25 Watts, and a mass loss rate of 1.5 x 10^-6 solar masses per year. The study has also used a nebular absorption line spectrum from the pulsar's surrounding environment, suggesting the presence of an accretion disk, a common feature in millisecond pulsars. The research has further been used to assess the capabilities of future telescopes for detecting the scattering environments surrounding pulsars similar to PSR B1133+16, with the Square Kilometre Array likely capable of detecting such phenomena, while the next generation Very Large Array may only be capable of detecting those pulsars with the closest scattering screens. To better capture speech's complex, quasi-periodic characteristics, a cascaded network architecture was introduced in a previous study, demonstrating superior performance compared to a single network. Building on this work, a revised cascaded network is presented here, featuring a two-stage structure where frequency information is extracted in the initial network, serving as input to the second network. This simple, efficient design surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of spectral distance and achieves near-optimal recognition rates in speech analysis, even without utilizing traditional features like mel-frequency filtering. The benefits of this cascaded architecture are highlighted through a detailed performance comparison with its single-network counterpart and leading existing methods, including deep neural networks. The success of this model has been evaluated across multiple tasks and with different speech data, ensuring the efficacy of this design is robust and scalable. The project's code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/yangzw123/CascadedDNN. The improved cascaded network presents a concise, high-performance solution for processing speech and other quasi-periodic signals. This paper introduces the Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN), a novel method that enhances hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) by incorporating a graph convolutional neural network within a Lorentzian distance framework. Our research demonstrates that LGCN successfully improves existing hyperbolic GCNs by refining node feature representations. Additionally, LGCN achieves superior performance in comparison to HCNN and CGNH for node classification and graph classification tasks using various real-world datasets. More significantly, LGCN is shown to outperform state-of-the-art Euclidean GCNs, surpassing their performance by a significant margin of 8% in NLP-based graph classification and 12% in COMYE-based graph classification, respectively. This advancement is attributed to its ability to effectively leverage non-Euclidean distance metrics, resulting in a substantial improvement in model performance. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. Moreover, we propose a practical Lorentzian distance metric learning method and contribute a comprehensive hyperbolic GCN open-source dataset framework for the community. This framework encompasses six datasets across different categories for hyperbolic GCN evaluation, and it is accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. This research paves the way for further exploration of hyperbolic GCNs and provides a valuable resource for the field. This study focuses on solving the inverse problem of determining the unknown boundary condition in a Dirichlet problem for the Stokes system given partial and faulty measurements. As the quality of the available data deteriorates, solutions to the regularized optimization problem converge to a stable, observable state. The Stokes system's observability inequality is the key to achieving stability results in inverse problems. However, due to the frequent occurrence of ill-posedness, this issue is particularly critical for Stokes system inverse problems. A numerical example demonstrating the proposed method's performance completes the study. The results shown highlight the significance of accurate regularization, data, and the introduction of an additional stability term in achieving a stable and accurate solution. The challenge of determining unknown boundary conditions in the Stokes system with a partially known domain is also addressed, and the results are compared to existing research on similar problems. The proposed regularization strategy is validated visually and numerically. The study's data and results are available at [https://doi.org/10.7910/DV58TC], along with the numerical code at [https://doi.org/10.7910/DV58TD]. The discussion that follows can be found at [https://doi.org/10.7910/DV58TH]. The Tsallis distribution has extensive applications in various fields and is often used to describe irregularities and uncertainties. In physics, it is primarily linked to temperature fluctuations and other phenomena involving diversity. Beyond physics, the Tsallis distribution plays a significant role in modeling self-organizational properties and patterns in social systems. In this paper, we present a mathematical derivation of the Tsallis distribution by combining the law of large numbers with the concept of an average, which is relevant to decision-making processes in social systems. We then explore the distribution's properties and oddities in a way that is easily understood and related to its original Tsallis form. Additionally, we provide a clear explanation of how the Tsallis distribution can be viewed as a result of applying the average concept to random choices, which reflects the self-referential nature of the Tsallis distribution. We also discuss its connections to power laws and discuss possible interpretations of the distribution's width parameter. Furthermore, we propose a Tsallis-like distribution as a model for combining different opinions in social systems, which we test on real-world data involving Wikipedia editor collaborations. This new distribution provides a better fit to the data than existing models and offers insights into the Tsallis distribution's applications in physics and biology. We also explore its connection to the Pareto principle and 80-20 rule, known as the law of small numbers. This paper offers a interdisciplinary approach to understanding the Tsallis distribution through the lens of physics, biology, economics, and Wikipedia editor collaborations. A comprehensive theoretical analysis of the effective spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides is presented, with a focus on understanding how interaction effects and crystal field splitting influence this behavior. This research develops a comprehensive understanding of the effective spin-orbit coupling, beginning with an examination of its fundamental principles via multi-orbital Hartree-Fock simulations. It then explores various scenarios of increasing complexity, including a single S or M d-orbital, and later the relevant d-orbitals in transition metal oxides, both in isolated ions and within the strong coupling limit of Hartree-Fock. By applying a perturbative approach to the Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian, the research uncovers how the spin-orbit coupling can be expressed in terms of the orbital angular momentum operators, allowing for a clear separation of the direct and indirect components of spin-orbit coupling. It also demonstrates that the effective spin-orbit coupling can be viewed as a weighted average of the direct component and the indirect component, which is opposed by the crystal field splitting, leading to a Gaussian-like distribution with means and standard deviations specific to each transition metal oxide. Notably, the research reveals that the distribution of effective spin-orbit coupling is broadly divided into three categories: strong coupling (e.g., Ru and Os-based systems with indirect coupling dominant), intermediate coupling (e.g., Mn and Re-based systems with both direct and indirect coupling evenly balanced), and weak coupling (e.g., Fe and Ag-based systems with direct coupling dominant), offering valuable insights into the complex behavior of spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides. It also highlights the limitations of the perturbative approach in certain scenarios, such as strong interaction effects or weak coupling, and suggests that the research can be extended further by considering weak interaction effects, strong coupling limits, and periodic crystals using the perturbative method. It is anticipated that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the effective spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides, with implications for the behavior of these materials in various scenarios. It is also expected to provide a useful framework for predicting the effective spin-orbit coupling in previously unexamined transition metal oxides. It is further expected to influence ongoing and future experiments with spin-orbit coupled systems, such as optical and magnetic experiments with Ru-based and Os-based systems, and superconducting systems with Fe-based and Re-based materials. It is also expected to influence theoretical research on the behavior of spin-orbit coupled systems, such as the magnetic properties of Ru-based and Os-based systems

ViDaExpert is an advanced data visualization tool designed to facilitate the
understanding of complex datasets consisting of multiple variables. This expert
system, developed using Rule-Based Systems, provides several innovative features
to effectively present data in various dimensions. These features include the
capability to characterize data clusters, illustrate data distributions, and
visualize data points for easy analysis. With ViDaExpert, users can: (1) examine
data clusters and obtain specific insights, (2) explore dimension-specific data
and discover notable patterns, (3) visualize high-dimensional data for clear
insights, (4) compare two datasets for differences and similarities, (5)
examine correlation between variables, (6) visualize data distributions for each
dimension, (7) represent missing values for priority handling. This system's
advantages are demonstrated through an illustrative example involving a real-
world dataset from the healthcare industry. Overall, ViDaExpert presents a
user-friendly interface for exploring and visualizing multiple-variable data. 
The system's source code is available at https://github.com/RubinaYasmeen/ViDaExpert. 
This project is an original contribution to the field of data visualization, 
especially for datasets with multiple variables, and the source code is openly 
available for further modification and improvement.
